slides.explanation:
This is the roadmap for Lectures 1 and 2. You will move from **what biology is** and how it grew as a science, to **modern biology**, and then to the big question of the lecture: **what makes something alive?**

The last part, the characteristics of living things, is the most exam-relevant section of this lecture, so keep it in mind as the goal while you read.

slides.explanation:
Science is two things at once: a **body of knowledge** (what we already know) and a **method** for finding out new things (observing, questioning, testing).

The word **biology** comes from two Greek words: **bios** = life and **logos** = thought or study. So biology literally means *the study of life*.

Exam tip: be able to split the word into its Greek roots and give their meanings.

slides.explanation:
This slide tells the story of how life came to exist on Earth, in order:

- The universe began with the **Big Bang**, expanding from a tiny point.
- Earth is the only planet we know that holds life.
- Early Earth was hot, full of poisonous gases, with no free oxygen or liquid water.
- Life arose slowly through **chemical reactions** and gradual change.
- Life truly begins when a **cell** forms; organisms then went from single-celled to multicellular.
- **Survival of the fittest** (natural selection) shaped which forms lasted.

slides.explanation:
Biology did not start in a laboratory. More than **30,000 years ago**, people in France and Spain painted animals on cave walls. These paintings show that early humans were already **observing living things carefully**: their shapes, their behaviour and which ones mattered for survival.

The point for you: observation is the oldest tool in biology.

slides.explanation:
Early humans survived by **hunting animals** and later **growing crops**. To do that well they had to understand animal behaviour, including which predators were dangerous.

They had no labs, equipment or microscopes. All of their knowledge came from **using their senses**: looking, listening, touching and remembering. This is biology in its simplest form.

slides.explanation:
About **10,000 years ago** people began farming. Farming forced them to learn a lot about living things: when to plant seeds, how much water crops need, what to feed animals and how long animals live.

Because they were studying living things to make decisions, the slide calls these early farmers the first **biologists**. Knowledge was growing from practical need.

slides.explanation:
As people kept observing, they started asking organised questions: what do living things have in common, how are they different, why are they found where they are, and which environment suits which group?

The answers led to three early branches of knowledge:

- **Classification** (grouping living things)
- **Ecology** (living things and their environment)
- **Cultivation** (growing plants and raising animals)

Later came deeper questions about what living things are **made of** and how they are **organised**.

slides.explanation:
**Modern biology** began in the **17th century**, when people finally had the knowledge, skills and instruments (especially the microscope) to look closer.

- **William Harvey** (~1628) described how blood circulates around the body.
- **Robert Hooke** (~1665) first saw cell walls in cork and named them cells.
- **Anton van Leeuwenhoek** (~1674) saw living cells, which he called “very little animalcules”.

The questions changed from *what is it?* to *what do the parts do and how do they work?* Exam tip: match each scientist to their discovery and date.

slides.explanation:
Biology today is a **vast science**. More than **1.5 million species** have been described, and many more are still undiscovered.

It also has huge practical uses: **vaccines, medicines, agriculture, the human genome** and **cloning**. Because the subject is so large, it is divided into **subdivisions** (the next two slides) so each part can be studied in depth.

slides.explanation:
Another way to divide biology is by **the approach or question asked**, whatever the organism:

- **Taxonomy**: classifying and naming organisms
- **Morphology**: external form and structure
- **Anatomy**: internal structure
- **Physiology**: how the parts function
- **Cytology**: cells
- **Ecology**: organisms and their environment
- **Genetics**: inheritance
- **Pathology**: diseases

A common confusion: **morphology is outside form, anatomy is inside structure**, and **physiology is function**, not structure.

slides.explanation:
Biology has a few big ideas that connect every topic. These are called **unifying themes**:

- **Hierarchical organisation**: life is built in levels, from small and simple to large and complex (atom to cell to organism to biosphere).
- **Cell theory**: all organisms are made of cells.
- **Heredity**: information passes from parents to offspring.
- **Evolution**: populations change over time.

The next slide continues the list.

slides.explanation:
More unifying themes of biology:

- **Regulation**: to survive and reproduce, organisms must control their internal environment (this idea returns as homeostasis later in the course).
- **Structure and function**: the shape of a part matches its job.
- **Environmental interactions**: organisms interact with their own species and with the wider community.
- **Energy flow**: energy moves through food chains, cycles through ecosystems and changes form inside cells.

Together with the previous slide, these are the themes that tie the whole course together.

slides.title: So… Biology: Redefined
notes: Biology was first defined as the science that deals with the study of life
However, as we learn more, we see that biology involves many other things. It is also a study of all those things that affect life.
Thus the following is a more accurate definition of biology:
Biology is the study of living things and the things that were once alive, together with the matter and energy that surround them.

slides.explanation:
The first definition, *the study of life*, turned out to be too narrow. Living things depend on non-living things around them, such as water, air, sunlight and dead organic matter.

So the slide gives a **more complete definition**: biology is the study of **living things and things that were once alive**, together with the **matter and energy** around them.

Exam tip: this fuller definition is worth learning word for word.

slides.explanation:
What separates a human, an animal or a plant from a stone, a laptop or a phone? A laptop can process information and a phone can respond to touch, but neither is alive.

This slide sets up the question the rest of the lecture answers: **what special characteristics do all living things share?** No single feature is enough; living things show **all** of them together.

slides.explanation:
Every organism needs **energy**, and the **Sun** is the ultimate source. Energy passes up an **energy pyramid**:

- **Primary producers** (green plants) make food using sunlight.
- **Primary consumers** (herbivores) eat producers.
- **Secondary consumers** feed on primary consumers.
- **Tertiary consumers** feed on secondary consumers.

Note: the slide says secondary consumers eat both producers and primary consumers. That describes omnivores; most textbooks simply say secondary consumers eat primary consumers. Energy is lost at each level, which is why the pyramid narrows.

slides.explanation:
**Movement** is easy to see in animals, but plants move too, just more slowly:

- buds opening
- leaves turning towards the sun
- **Mimosa pudica** (the sensitive plant) folding its leaves when touched
- the **sundew**, a carnivorous plant whose sticky tentacles curl around trapped insects

So movement does not always mean moving from place to place; it includes movement of parts.

slides.explanation:
**Locomotion** is a special kind of movement: the organism **moves itself** from one place to another (self-propulsion), for example by swimming, running, flying or walking. Even microorganisms can propel themselves.

But not every change of position counts. Wind moving tree branches is not locomotion, because the tree is not moving itself.

Exam tip: movement includes moving parts; locomotion means moving the whole body by its own effort.

All living things are made of **cells**, the basic unit of life. The slide shows three examples: a **plant cell**, an **animal cell** and a **bacterial cell**.

They differ in details (plant cells have cell walls and chloroplasts; bacterial cells have no nucleus), but they are all cells. This idea is the **cell theory** from the unifying themes, and it is covered in detail in Lectures 8–9.

slides.explanation:
**Protoplasm** is the living material inside cells: a complex mixture of water, carbohydrates, fats, proteins and other substances. All living cells have it.

Its composition is **not fixed**: it differs between organisms, between parts of the same organism, and changes over time.

Living things **organise**: matter into protoplasm, protoplasm into cells, and cells into a whole body. That organising ability is why living things are called **organisms**.

slides.explanation:
**Growth** in living things is more than getting bigger. A crystal or a pile of sand can get bigger by adding material, but that is not biological growth.

True growth means the organism **builds new living material** (protoplasm), **increases its number of cells** by reproducing them, and moves from one stage of life to the next.

slides.explanation:
**Development** is the series of changes an organism goes through as it grows towards its final (adult) form, for example a seed becoming a tree or a larva becoming a butterfly.

Through development, cells become **specialised** into different parts, and the organism becomes a unique individual.

Exam tip: growth is about increase; development is about change and specialisation.

slides.explanation:
Even when an organism seems to have stopped growing, it keeps working to **maintain and repair** itself. This is part of growth and development.

Examples from the slide:

- dead skin cells being replaced
- a cut finger healing
- a house lizard regrowing its tail

Without constant maintenance and repair, the body would wear out quickly.

slides.explanation:
Only living things can **reproduce**, making offspring similar to themselves. The method varies: laying eggs, giving birth, or seeds growing into new plants.

The slide gives two laws of nature to remember:

- **“Life produces life”**: living things only come from other living things.
- **“Like produces like”**: offspring resemble their parents.

slides.explanation:
Every organism has a limited **life span**, and it varies hugely: humans about 70 years, horses about 30 years, some plants more than 1,000 years (like the California redwoods in the figure).

Because individuals die, a species survives only if it produces offspring: **limited life span → offspring → reproduction**. Reproduction is also an **energy-requiring** process.

slides.explanation:
**Irritability** means the ability to **respond to stimuli** (changes in the surroundings).

- **Animals** have a nervous system and sense organs (eyes, nose, ears), so they respond quickly.
- **Plants** have no nervous system; they respond slowly, for example to light, oxygen or nutrients.
- **Microorganisms**, even single-celled ones, respond to nutrients and conditions around them.

So every living thing responds, just at different speeds.

slides.explanation:
Responding to stimuli involves two more ideas:

- **Coordination**: doing the right thing at the right time, with different parts working together.
- **Behaviour**: responding to a stimulus in a regular, recognisable pattern.

For example, a bird flying away when a cat appears shows both: senses, muscles and brain work together (coordination) in a typical pattern (behaviour).

Variation:
Changes occur as a result of characteristic.
> Most variations do not affect an organism's chances of survival
• Give an organism a better chance of surviving in a changing environment

The process by which a certain type of organisms becomes better suited to survive

slides.explanation:
**Variation** means that individuals of the same kind are not identical; they differ in their characteristics. Most variations do not change an individual's chance of survival, but some give it an advantage when the environment changes.

**Adaptation** is the process by which a type of organism becomes **better suited to survive** in its environment. Examples:

- **Hibernation**: surviving winter in a deep sleep.
- **Mimicry**: the viceroy butterfly looks like the bitter-tasting monarch, so predators avoid it too.

slides.explanation:
**Metabolism** is the sum of **all the chemical processes** in an organism: the exchange of matter and energy with the surroundings and inside the body.

The slide lists the processes it includes:

- **Ingestion**: taking in food
- **Digestion**: breaking it down
- **Assimilation**: using the products to build the body
- **Respiration**: releasing energy from food
- **Excretion**: removing waste

slides.explanation:
Metabolism has two opposite phases:

- **Anabolism**: **building up** complex molecules from simpler ones. It uses energy (for example, making proteins from amino acids).
- **Catabolism**: **breaking down** complex molecules into simpler ones. It releases energy (for example, breaking down glucose in respiration).

The roadmap for this lecture, in order: what classification is, how people classified living things before and after Linnaeus, **binomial nomenclature** (two-word scientific names), the **genus and species** concept, why scientific names matter, the **seven main taxa**, the different **kingdom systems**, and finally the modern **phylogenetic (three-domain)** system.

The taxa order and the kingdom systems are the most commonly examined parts.

slides.explanation:
Why classify at all? Because there are so many kinds of living things:

- about **2 million** kinds may exist today,
- about **1.5 million** have been identified,
- for every living kind, roughly **400 more** once lived and are now extinct,
- so perhaps **1 billion** kinds have existed over Earth's history.

Nobody could study that many organisms one by one. Grouping them makes the variety manageable.

slides.explanation:
**Classification** is the grouping of similar things for a specific purpose. You already use it every day: a supermarket groups products, a stamp collector groups stamps by country, a dictionary lists words alphabetically.

Biological classification does the same for organisms. The lecture splits its history into **early** classification (before Linnaeus) and **modern** classification (Linnaeus onwards).

slides.explanation:
The earliest humans classified by **usefulness**: plants versus animals, edible versus poisonous plants, harmful versus harmless animals.

Around **300 BC, Aristotle** built the first formal system. Only about 1,000 kinds of organisms were known, and his system lasted almost **2,000 years**. By the early **18th century** more than **10,000** kinds were known, far too many for Aristotle's system, so a new one was needed. That new system came from Linnaeus (next slide).

slides.explanation:
**Taxonomy** is the science of classifying organisms.

**Carolus Linnaeus** (18th century) is the father of modern classification. He grouped organisms by **structural similarity**: organisms with very similar structures were placed in the same **species**. So all modern humans form one species, all house cats form one species, and all sugar maples form one species.

The slide also defines **diversity** as the number of kinds of living things, which is exactly what classification tries to organise.

slides.explanation:
After classifying, Linnaeus gave every organism a **two-word name**: this is **binomial nomenclature**. The names are in **Latin**, so scientists everywhere use the same name.

The first word is the **genus**, the second is the **species**. Humans are *Homo sapiens*. Writing rules:

- printed: *italic* (genus capitalised, species lowercase)
- handwritten: each word **underlined separately**

Note: the slide gives the cat as *Felis domesticus*; most modern sources use *Felis catus*. For the exam, follow your lecture.

slides.explanation:
The two words in a scientific name are two levels of classification:

- **Genus** (plural *genera*): a group of **similar species**. All maples belong to the genus *Acer*: sugar maple *Acer saccharum*, silver maple *Acer saccharinum*, red maple *Acer rubrum*.
- **Species** (plural also *species*): organisms that are structurally very similar and can **interbreed naturally to produce fertile offspring**.

Exam tip: the interbreeding definition of species is the one to write in short answers.

slides.explanation:
Common names cause confusion. One animal, *Felis concolor*, is called cougar, mountain lion, puma, panther and more. The domestic cow has a different name in every language: *la vache* (French), *die Kuh* (German), *la vaca* (Spanish), *goru* (Bengali).

A scientific name like ***Bos taurus*** is the **same everywhere**, so scientists always know exactly which organism is meant. That is the whole reason for scientific names.

There are **seven main taxa** (classification groups), from broadest to most specific:

**Kingdom → Phylum → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species**

Each level contains fewer, more similar organisms. A common memory aid: **K**ing **P**hilip **C**ame **O**ver **F**or **G**ood **S**oup.

Exam tip: questions often ask for the correct order, or which taxon comes between two others.

Modern biologists classify using evidence beyond outward appearance:

- **Homologous structures**: parts with the same basic pattern, the same relationship to other parts and the same development, even if they look different (a human arm, a bat wing and a whale flipper).
- **Similar biochemistry**: closely related organisms make similar chemical compounds.
- **Genetic similarity**: the more similar the DNA, the more closely related the organisms are likely to be.

These all point towards shared ancestry, which leads to the phylogenetic system.

slides.explanation:
**Carl Woese** introduced a completely new approach. He compared **rRNA sequences** (ribosomal RNA), which change very slowly over evolution, to measure how closely organisms are related.

This **phylogenetic** (evolution-based) system puts all life into **three domains**:

1. **Eukarya** (organisms with a nucleus: animals, plants, fungi, protists)
2. **Bacteria**
3. **Archaea** (prokaryotes that often live in extreme places)

The domain is a level **above** kingdom.

slides.explanation:
This slide walks through **your own classification**, starting at the top:

- **Kingdom Animalia**: multicellular organisms that **ingest** food rather than make it.
- **Phylum**: animals with a **backbone** (vertebral column) or a dorsal hollow nerve cord protecting the central nervous system.

The slide labels this level *Vertebrata*; strictly, humans are in phylum **Chordata** (as slide 11 shows), subphylum Vertebrata.

slides.explanation:
Continuing down the human classification:

- **Class Mammalia**: vertebrates with **mammary glands**, **hair or fur** and placental development.
- **Order Primates**: mammals adapted to life in trees, with **opposable thumbs** (the thumb can touch the other fingers, allowing grasping).

Further down:

- **Family Hominidae**: primates that move mainly by **bipedal** (two-footed) locomotion.
- **Genus *Homo***: hominids with **large brain cases** (skulls).

Walking upright and a large brain are the two traits that separate our branch from the other primates.

The genus *Homo* has had **several species**, most now extinct. The slide lists them roughly in order of appearance: *H. habilis* (the “handy man”), *H. rudolfensis*, *H. ergaster*, *H. erectus* (“upright man”), *H. heidelbergensis*, *H. rhodesiensis*, *H. neanderthalensis* (Neanderthals) and finally *H. sapiens*.

Humans are defined by a combination of traits from each level: **bipedal** (family), **opposable thumbs** (order) and a **large brain case** (genus).

slides.explanation:
Everything your body does is chemistry. When you eat food or breathe in oxygen, your cells use those materials in **chemical reactions** that keep you alive.

The slide's analogy: buildings are made of bricks, steel and glass; living things are made of **chemical compounds**. Just as an architect must understand building materials, every kind of biologist must understand the chemistry that living things are built from.

slides.explanation:
Is fat always bad? No. The body needs a little fat every day (the slide says about a tablespoon) for energy, cell membranes and absorbing some vitamins.

The problem in many developed countries is eating far too much, which contributes to obesity. But the slide's key message is the last line: **the kind of fat you eat can matter more than the total amount**. That difference comes down to chemistry, as the next slide shows.

slides.explanation:
**Trans fats** are fats in which the hydrogen atoms around a carbon-carbon double bond sit on **opposite sides** of the chain. This shape makes them behave like saturated fat in the body.

They are made when vegetable oils are **partially hydrogenated**. Even about **2 g a day** raises the risk of **atherosclerosis** (hardening of the arteries), heart attack and diabetes, and one small serving of fries cooked in such oil can hold about 5 g.

So a small change in how atoms are arranged has a big effect on health. That is why we learn chemistry.

slides.explanation:
Key definitions:

- **Atom**: the fundamental building block of matter.
- **Atomic number**: the number of **protons** in the nucleus. It decides which element the atom is.
- **Charge**: an electrical property of some particles. **Opposite charges attract, like charges repel.**
- **Electron**: a **negative** particle that moves in orbitals around the nucleus.
- **Element**: a pure substance made only of atoms with the **same number of protons**.

More key definitions:

- **Isotopes**: forms of the same element with different numbers of **neutrons**.
- **Mass number**: protons + neutrons.
- **Neutron**: an **uncharged** particle in the nucleus.
- **Nucleus**: the core of the atom, holding protons and neutrons.
- **Proton**: a **positive** particle in the nucleus.
- **Radioisotope**: an isotope with an **unstable** nucleus.
- **Radioactive decay**: a radioisotope's nucleus breaking down and giving off energy and particles.

Exam tip: atomic number counts protons only; mass number counts protons plus neutrons.

slides.explanation:
Three facts about atoms:

- An atom is **electrically neutral**.
- That is because it has the **same number of electrons (–) as protons (+)**, so the charges cancel.
- The number of protons is **fixed** for a given element. Change the proton number and you have a different element.

Electrons, on the other hand, can be gained or lost, which is how ions form (slide 13).

slides.explanation:
**Isotopes** of an element have the same number of protons but **different numbers of neutrons**. Carbon is the example:

- **Carbon-12**: 6 protons, 6 neutrons
- **Carbon-13**: 6 protons, 7 neutrons
- **Carbon-14**: 6 protons, 8 neutrons

All three are carbon because they have 6 protons. The number after the name is the **mass number**. Carbon-14 is a radioisotope, used in carbon dating.

slides.explanation:
An **ion** is an atom (or group of atoms) with a **net positive or negative charge**. During chemical reactions the protons stay the same; only **electrons** are lost or gained.

- **Losing** electrons → more protons than electrons → a **positive ion (cation)**.
- **Gaining** electrons → more electrons than protons → a **negative ion (anion)**.

Memory tip: ca**t**ion has a **t** that looks like a plus sign.

slides.explanation:
Worked example of ions:

- **Na⁺** (sodium ion): 11 protons, 10 electrons. It lost one electron, so it is a **cation** with a +1 charge.
- **Cl⁻** (chloride ion): 17 protons, 18 electrons. It gained one electron, so it is an **anion** with a –1 charge.

Sodium gives its electron to chlorine, and the opposite charges attract. That is the ionic bond in table salt (slide 21).

A **molecule** is at least two atoms joined in a **definite arrangement** by chemical bonds.

- The atoms can be the **same element** (O₂, H₂) or **different elements** (H₂O, glucose C₆H₁₂O₆).
- They join in a **fixed ratio** (water is always 2 H to 1 O).
- Like atoms, molecules are **electrically neutral**.

**Element vs compound**:

- An **element** cannot be broken down into other substances by chemical reactions. Each has a symbol of one or two letters, e.g. C (carbon), Co (cobalt), H (hydrogen).
- A **compound** is made of **two or more different elements in a fixed ratio**. Sodium chloride (NaCl) contains sodium and chlorine in a 1:1 ratio.

Note: every compound is made of molecules or ions, but not every molecule is a compound (O₂ is a molecule of an element).

Why do atoms bond at all? An atom is most **stable** when its **outermost electron shell is full** (no vacancies). Atoms with vacancies interact with other atoms: they **give up, take or share electrons** until the outer shell is full.

- Giving or taking electrons → **ionic bonds**.
- Sharing electrons → **covalent bonds**.

slides.explanation:
An **ionic bond** forms when one atom **transfers** electrons from its outer shell to another atom.

- The atom that gives up electrons becomes a **cation** (+).
- The atom that receives them becomes an **anion** (–).
- The opposite charges attract strongly, holding them together.

Ionic bonds are **strong**. Example: **NaCl**, table salt.

When an ionic compound like NaCl dissolves in **water**, it breaks apart into separate ions (Na⁺ and Cl⁻). This is **ionisation**.

slides.explanation:
A **covalent bond** forms when atoms **share** outer-shell electrons instead of transferring them. This happens when neither atom can easily give up or take electrons.

Examples: **O₂** and **H₂**, where two identical atoms share electrons. Covalent bonds hold together almost all the molecules of life (water, sugars, proteins, DNA).

**Electronegativity** is how strongly an atom pulls **shared electrons** in a covalent bond towards itself.

A **hydrogen bond** is a **weak attraction** between a slightly positive hydrogen atom (already in a polar covalent bond) and a slightly negative atom such as oxygen or nitrogen in another polar bond.

- Like ionic bonds, it is an attraction between opposite charges.
- Unlike ionic bonds, it does **not** join atoms into molecules, so it is not a true chemical bond.
- It forms and breaks **easily**.

Hydrogen bonds hold water molecules together and hold the two strands of DNA together.

slides.explanation:
Water's **polar covalent bonds** (and the hydrogen bonds between molecules) give it the properties life depends on:

- **Excellent solvent**: dissolves many substances. **Hydrophilic** substances mix with water; **hydrophobic** ones (like oils) do not.
- **Stable temperature**: water absorbs a lot of heat before its temperature changes, which keeps bodies and oceans stable.
- **Ice floats**: hydrogen bonds hold ice molecules further apart, so ice is less dense than liquid water.
- **Cohesion and adhesion**: water sticks to itself and to other surfaces.
- **Evaporation** cools surfaces (like sweat).

slides.explanation:
**Diffusion** is the movement of molecules from an area of **high concentration** to an area of **low concentration**, until they are evenly spread.

It needs no energy; molecules move by random motion. Example: a drop of ink spreading through water, or oxygen moving from the lungs into the blood.

This figure shows diffusion across a **membrane**:

- (a) If the substance **can pass through** the membrane (penetrating solute), it diffuses across until the concentration is equal on both sides.
- (b) If the membrane is **impermeable** to it (non-penetrating solute), no diffusion occurs, however big the difference.

This idea sets up osmosis, where only water can cross.

**Osmosis** is the **diffusion of water across a (semi-permeable) membrane**.

Water moves towards the side with **more solute**, because that side has a **lower concentration of water**. In other words, water moves from dilute to concentrated solution.

slides.explanation:
**Tonicity** describes how a solution affects the movement of water into or out of a cell. It depends on the concentration of solutes that **cannot cross** the membrane, compared with inside the cell. It has no units.

- **Isotonic**: equal solute on both sides; water moves both ways with no net change.
- **Hypotonic** (*hypo* = less): less solute outside, so water moves **into** the cell.
- **Hypertonic** (*hyper* = more): more solute outside, so water moves **out of** the cell.

The slide's shortcut: water follows the salt.

slides.explanation:
What tonicity does to real cells:

- **Animal cells** (like red blood cells): hypotonic → swell and burst (**lysed**); isotonic → **normal**; hypertonic → **shrivel**.
- **Plant cells** (with a cell wall): hypotonic → **turgid** (firm, the normal healthy state); isotonic → **flaccid** (limp); hypertonic → **plasmolysed** (the membrane pulls away from the wall).

Notice the plant cell's wall stops it bursting, so its ideal state is hypotonic.

slides.explanation:
**Acids and bases**:

- **Acids** release hydrogen ions (H⁺) in water; **bases** accept them. **Salts** release other ions.
- **pH** measures acidity on a **logarithmic** scale: **7 is neutral**, below 7 is acidic, above 7 is basic (alkaline). pH = –log₁₀[H⁺]. Each step of 1 is a **tenfold** change.
- A **buffer** resists changes in pH when acid or base is added. It usually contains a weak acid or base plus its salt.

Buffers keep blood pH stable (about 7.4), which is part of **homeostasis**. The slide also lists sources of acidity in the environment: fossil fuels, nitrogen fertilisers and acid rain.

slides.explanation: Lectures 6–7 are about **biological macromolecules**: the four big families of large molecules that living things are built from. They are **carbohydrates, proteins, lipids** and **nucleic acids**. This lecture uses the chemistry from Lectures 4–5 (covalent bonds, hydrogen bonds, water) all the time.

slides.explanation:
Life is **carbon-based**. Carbon can form four bonds, so it builds long chains and rings. Together with a few other elements (hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, phosphorus, sulfur), carbon compounds **assemble into complex forms**.

These large assemblies are the **building blocks of living organisms**: the membranes, enzymes, energy stores and genetic material of every cell.

- **Polymerisation** is linking monomers together to form a polymer.
- The linking happens through a **condensation reaction** (also called **dehydration synthesis**): two molecules join with a new covalent bond, and a small molecule, usually **water**, is removed.

Building polymers **requires an input of energy**. This is an **anabolic** process (building up), from the metabolism section of Lectures 1–2.

slides.explanation:
**Hydrolysis** is the **reverse of condensation**. Water is added to break the bonds between monomers, splitting a polymer into smaller pieces (*hydro* = water, *lysis* = splitting).

Breaking these bonds **releases energy**, returning some of the energy that was used to build the polymer. This is **catabolism** (breaking down). Digestion of food is mostly hydrolysis.

Exam tip: condensation removes water and builds; hydrolysis adds water and breaks.

slides.explanation:
**Carbohydrates** have the general formula **(CH₂O)ₙ**: carbon, hydrogen and oxygen in a **1:2:1 ratio**. The most common is **glucose**, C₆H₁₂O₆, which is (CH₂O)₆.

Their jobs: **structural materials** (cellulose), and **storing and transporting energy** (glucose, starch, glycogen).

There are **three types**: **monosaccharides** (single sugars), **oligosaccharides** (a few sugars joined, including disaccharides) and **polysaccharides** (long chains).

slides.explanation:
Four polysaccharides and their roles:

- **Starch**: energy storage in **plants**. Animals can digest it.
- **Glycogen**: energy storage in **animals** (in liver and muscle). Also digestible.
- **Cellulose**: a **structural** component of plant cell walls. Its glucose units are joined by a different type of bond, so **animals cannot digest it** (it becomes dietary fibre).
- **Chitin**: contains nitrogen as well as sugar; it forms the **exoskeletons of insects** (and fungal cell walls).

Exam tip: starch is plant storage, glycogen is animal storage.

slides.explanation:
**Functions of carbohydrates**:

- **Energy**: the main and quickest fuel for cells.
- **Sparing protein**: if you eat enough carbohydrate, the body does not have to break down protein for energy.
- **Preventing ketosis**: without enough carbohydrate the body burns fat heavily, producing ketone bodies.
- **Biological recognition**: sugars on cell surfaces help cells recognise each other.
- **Flavour and sweetness**.
- **Dietary fibre**: helps move waste through the gut.

**Proteins** are the **most diverse** macromolecules in both structure and function.

They are **polymers of amino acids**. Thousands of different proteins are made from only **20 kinds of amino acids**, just as thousands of words are made from 26 letters. The order of amino acids decides the protein's shape and job.

A **peptide bond** is the covalent bond that joins two amino acids. It forms by a **condensation reaction** between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of the next, releasing a molecule of **water**.

slides.explanation:
Proteins have **four levels of structure**:

1. **Primary**: the **sequence** (linear order) of amino acids.
2. **Secondary**: local folding or coiling held by hydrogen bonds, as **α-helices** and **β-pleated sheets**.
3. **Tertiary**: the protein's full **3-D shape**, from many interactions between R groups.
4. **Quaternary**: **two or more polypeptide chains** joined into one protein. Example: **haemoglobin** (four chains).

Exam tip: not every protein has quaternary structure, only those with more than one chain.

slides.explanation:
**Lipids** are made of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, but **not in a fixed ratio** like carbohydrates. Their building blocks are **fatty acids and glycerol**.

Key properties:

- They store the **most energy**: about **twice** as much per gram as carbohydrates.
- They are **not soluble in water** (hydrophobic) but dissolve in non-polar solvents.
- They are structurally varied.

Examples: **fats, oils, phospholipids, waxes, steroid hormones** and **triglycerides**.

slides.explanation:
A **triglyceride** is made from **one glycerol + three fatty acids**, joined by condensation.

Fatty acids can be:

- **Saturated**: no double bonds between carbons; straight chains that pack tightly.
- **Unsaturated**: one or more double bonds; kinked chains that pack loosely.

This controls the melting point: **the more unsaturated, the lower the melting point**, so unsaturated fats tend to be liquid (oils) at room temperature.

slides.explanation:
**Phospholipids** are like a triglyceride in which **one fatty acid is replaced by a phosphate group** (with extra groups attached).

This gives the molecule two personalities, making it **amphipathic**:

- the **phosphate head** is **hydrophilic** (water-loving)
- the two **fatty acid tails** are **hydrophobic** (water-fearing)

This is exactly what lets phospholipids form **cell membranes** (next slide).

In water, phospholipids arrange themselves into a **bilayer**: two layers with the **hydrophilic heads facing outward** (towards water on both sides) and the **hydrophobic tails tucked inside**, away from water.

This bilayer is the basic structure of every **cell membrane**. The figure also shows that saturated tails pack tightly while a mix with unsaturated (kinked) tails packs loosely, making the membrane more fluid.

slides.explanation:
In DNA, the amount of **adenine equals thymine**, and **guanine equals cytosine** (Chargaff's rule).

Why? Because the two strands are held together by **complementary base pairing** through hydrogen bonds: **A always pairs with T** and **G always pairs with C**. Every A on one strand is matched by a T on the other, so their totals must be equal. The slide also notes that DNA's secondary structure (the helix) is held by hydrogen bonds, like a protein's.

slides.explanation:
**DNA vs RNA**, a classic comparison:

- **Function**: DNA stores and passes on genetic information long term; RNA carries the code from the nucleus to the ribosome so proteins can be made.
- **Structure**: DNA is usually **double-stranded** and long; RNA is usually **single-stranded** and shorter.
- **Sugar**: **deoxyribose** in DNA, **ribose** in RNA.
- **Bases**: DNA has **thymine**, RNA has **uracil** instead.
- **Pairing**: A–T and G–C in DNA; **A–U** and G–C in RNA.

slides.title: CELL STRUCTURE AND FUNCTION
notes: Cells
A cell is the smallest unit of life.
Cells can survive and reproduce on its own.
Some cells live and reproduce independently. Others do so as part of a multicelled organism.
Discovery of cells

In the middle of the 17th century, one of the pioneers of microscopy, Robert Hooke (1635–1703), decided to examine a piece of cork tissue with his home-built microscope. He saw numerous box shaped structures that he thought resembled row of empty boxes or rooms, so he called them ‘cells’.

slides.explanation:
A **cell** is the **smallest unit of life**: the smallest thing that can survive and reproduce on its own. Some cells live independently (bacteria, amoeba); others live as part of a multicellular organism.

Cells were discovered in the mid-17th century by **Robert Hooke**. Looking at thin slices of **cork** under his home-built microscope, he saw rows of box-like spaces that reminded him of small rooms, so he called them **cells**. (He was actually seeing the empty walls of dead plant cells.)

slides.explanation:
The **cell theory** has three parts:

1. Every organism is made of **one or more cells**.
2. The cell is the **smallest unit with the properties of life**.
3. New cells come only from the **growth and division of existing cells**, which gives continuity of life.

Biologists divide cells into two general types: **prokaryotic** and **eukaryotic**. Exam tip: the three statements of cell theory are a common short-answer question.

slides.explanation:
**Prokaryotic vs eukaryotic cells**:

- **Prokaryotes**: usually **unicellular**; **no true nucleus** (DNA sits in a region called the nucleoid); **no membrane-bound organelles**; **smaller ribosomes** (70S). Examples: **bacteria and archaea**.
- **Eukaryotes**: usually multicellular; a **membrane-bound nucleus**; **membrane-bound organelles** present; **larger ribosomes** (80S). Examples: **animals, plants, fungi, algae**.

*Pro* means before and *karyon* means nucleus, so prokaryotes are cells from before the nucleus; *eu* means true.

slides.title: STRUCTURE COMMON TO ALL CELLS: PLASMA MEMBRANE
notes: The plasma membrane is the boundary between the cell and its environment.
It isolates the cell, regulates what enters and leaves the cell.
It allows interaction with other cells. It comprises of lipids and proteins.
Lipid Bilayer
Lipids—mainly phospholipids—make up the bulk of a cell membrane.

A phospholipid consists of a phosphate containing head and two fatty acid tails. The polar head is hydrophilic, which means that it interacts with water molecules. The nonpolar tails are hydrophobic, so they do not interact with water molecules, but they do interact with the tails of other phospholipids.
Lipid bilayers are the basic structural and functional framework of all cell membranes, gives membrane it's fluidity

slides.explanation:
The **plasma membrane** is the boundary between the cell and its surroundings. It isolates the cell, **controls what enters and leaves**, and lets the cell interact with other cells. It is made of **lipids and proteins**.

The lipids are mainly **phospholipids** arranged in a **bilayer**: **hydrophilic (polar) heads** face the watery inside and outside, while **hydrophobic (non-polar) fatty acid tails** face each other in the middle. This **lipid bilayer** is the framework of all membranes and gives the membrane its **fluidity**. (Link back to phospholipids in Lectures 6–7.)

slides.title: FUNCTIONS OF PLASMA MEMBRANE
notes: A cell must exchange materials with its surroundings, a process controlled by the plasma membrane
Plasma membranes are selectively permeable, regulating the cell’s molecular traffic.
Hydrophobic (nonpolar) molecules, such as hydrocarbons, can dissolve in the lipid bilayer and pass through the membrane rapidly.

slides.explanation:
The plasma membrane controls the **exchange of materials** between the cell and its surroundings. It is **selectively permeable**: some substances cross easily, others cannot, so the membrane regulates the cell's traffic.

Small **hydrophobic (non-polar) molecules**, such as hydrocarbons, oxygen and carbon dioxide, dissolve in the lipid bilayer and pass through **quickly**. Ions and large polar molecules need help from membrane proteins.

notes: The nucleus is the defining organelle of eukaryotic cells.
The nucleus is separated from the cytoplasm by a double membrane (two phospholipid bilayers); known as the nuclear envelope.
The nuclear envelope controls the passage of molecules between the nucleus and cytoplasm.
The nucleus contains the DNA, the stored genetic instructions of each cell. In addition, important reactions for interpreting the genetic instructions occur in the nucleus.
In the nucleus, DNA is organized into discrete units called chromosomes
Each chromosome is composed of a single DNA molecule associated with proteins

slides.explanation:
The **nucleus** is the defining organelle of eukaryotic cells.

- It is surrounded by the **nuclear envelope**, a **double membrane** (two phospholipid bilayers) that controls what passes between the nucleus and cytoplasm.
- It holds the cell's **DNA**, the stored genetic instructions, and the reactions that begin reading those instructions happen here.
- The DNA is organised into **chromosomes**; each chromosome is **one DNA molecule plus proteins**.

Think of the nucleus as the cell's control centre and library.

slides.title: STRUCTURE COMMON TO ALL CELLS: RIBOSOMES
notes: Two types:
Bound ribosomes: Many ribosomes are attached to the endoplasmic reticulum. Areas of rough ER are active sites of protein production.

Free ribosomes: Many ribosomes are also found floating freely in the cytoplasm wherever proteins are being assembled. Cells that are actively producing protein (e.g., liver cells) have great numbers of free and attached ribosomes.
Ribosomes are non-membranous organelles responsible for the synthesis of proteins from amino acids.
They are composed of RNA and protein.
Each ribosome is composed of two subunits—a large one and a small one.

**Ribosomes** make **proteins** from amino acids. They are **not surrounded by a membrane**, are made of **RNA and protein**, and have **two subunits** (one large, one small).

There are two types:

- **Bound ribosomes**: attached to the endoplasmic reticulum, forming **rough ER**. These make proteins for membranes or for export from the cell.
- **Free ribosomes**: floating in the cytoplasm, making proteins used inside the cell.

Cells that make lots of protein, such as liver cells, have very many of both.

slides.title: STRUCTURE COMMON TO ALL CELLS: CYTOPLASM
notes: In prokaryotes, cytoplasm inside the membrane is a jelly-like substance comprises of water, enzymes and some proteins. It also contains the genetic material.
In eukaryotes, the cytoplasm is a network of fibers that organizes structures and activities in the cell and known as cytoskeleton.
Between the nucleus and plasma membrane of all eukaryotic cells is a system of interconnected protein filaments collectively called the cytoskeleton.
The cytoskeleton is a network of fibers extending throughout the cytoplasm. Elements of the cytoskeleton reinforce, organize, and move cell structures, anchoring many organelles.

The **cytoplasm** is everything inside the plasma membrane except the nucleus.

- In **prokaryotes**, it is a **jelly-like** fluid of water, enzymes and proteins, and it also contains the genetic material.
- In **eukaryotes**, a network of protein fibres runs through the cytoplasm: the **cytoskeleton**. It stretches between the nucleus and the plasma membrane, **supports, organises and moves** cell structures, and **anchors organelles** in place.

Note: the slide describes the eukaryotic cytoplasm as a network of fibres. More precisely, the cytoplasm contains this network (the cytoskeleton) within the cytosol.

slides.explanation:
The **endoplasmic reticulum (ER)** is part of the cell's **cytomembrane system**. It is an extension of the nuclear envelope that folds into flattened sacs and tubes, forming one continuous compartment where new polypeptide chains are modified.

- **Rough ER**: **ribosomes** on its surface make it look rough. Proteins made there enter it to be modified. Cells that **secrete proteins** have a lot of rough ER.
- **Smooth ER**: **no ribosomes**; this is where **lipids are assembled**.

**Functions of the ER**:

- **Smooth ER**: makes **lipids**, metabolises **carbohydrates**, **detoxifies drugs and poisons** (liver cells have a lot of it), and **stores calcium ions**.
- **Rough ER**: has **bound ribosomes**, sends proteins out in **transport vesicles** (small membrane bubbles), and acts as a **membrane factory** for the cell.

Exam tip: the four smooth ER functions are often asked as a list.

The processed molecules are packaged into membrane vesicles, then targeted and transported to their final destinations.

Modifies products of the ER
Manufactures certain macromolecules
Sorts and packages materials into transport vesicles.

slides.explanation:
The **Golgi apparatus (Golgi body)** is a stack of flattened membrane compartments. It **processes and packages** proteins that arrive from the rough ER, then sends them to where they are needed inside **membrane vesicles**.

Its functions:

- **modifies** products of the ER
- **manufactures** some macromolecules
- **sorts and packages** materials into transport vesicles

Think of it as the cell's post office.

- **Transport vesicles** from the ER arrive at the **cis face** (the receiving side).

slides.explanation:
**Vesicles** are small membrane-enclosed sacs. Two main types are covered here.

**Lysosomes** are the cell's **digestion and recycling centres**:

- They bud from the **Golgi bodies**.
- They contain powerful **enzymes** that break down carbohydrates, proteins, nucleic acids and lipids.
- These enzymes work best in the **acidic** interior of the lysosome.
- They break down **worn-out cell parts** and unwanted molecules so their pieces can be reused.

**Peroxisomes** are vesicles found in both plant and animal cells.

- Their enzymes digest **fatty acids and amino acids**.
- These reactions produce **hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂)**, which is toxic. Peroxisome enzymes convert it to **water and oxygen**, or use it to break down **alcohol and other toxins**.

Exam tip: lysosomes digest with acid enzymes; peroxisomes deal with fatty acids and hydrogen peroxide.

They have various enzymes to catalyze cellular respiration.
Cells that have a very high demand for energy tend to have many mitochondria e.g. liver needs more because needs more energy.
Mitochondria, like most organelles, can move within the cell and they grow and divide independently.

slides.explanation:
**Mitochondria** (singular: mitochondrion) are the organelles that make **ATP**, the cell's main energy molecule. They contain the enzymes of **cellular respiration**, which releases energy from food.

Cells with a high energy demand, such as **liver** and muscle cells, have **many mitochondria**. Mitochondria can move within the cell, and they **grow and divide on their own**, a clue to their bacterial origin (slide 27).

slides.explanation:
A mitochondrion has a **double membrane**:

- a **smooth outer membrane** facing the cytoplasm
- a **folded inner membrane**; the folds are called **cristae**. The reactions that make ATP happen here, and the folds give a large surface area for them.

The fluid inside the inner membrane is the matrix.

notes: Plastids are a category of membrane-enclosed organelles that function in photosynthesis or storage in plant and algal cells.
Plastids called chloroplasts are organelles specialized for photosynthesis which contain the green pigment chlorophyll, as well as enzymes and other molecules that function in photosynthesis.

slides.explanation:
**Plastids** are membrane-enclosed organelles in **plant and algal cells** used for **photosynthesis or storage**.

**Chloroplasts** are the plastids specialised for **photosynthesis**. They contain the green pigment **chlorophyll**, plus the enzymes and other molecules photosynthesis needs. Animal cells do not have chloroplasts.

slides.title: ENERGY RELATED ORGANELLE: CHLOROPLAST
notes: Chloroplast structure includes
Stroma: Each has two outer membranes enclosing a semifluid interior, the stroma, that contains enzymes and the chloroplast‘s own
DNA.

Thylakoids: Inside the stroma, a third, highly folded membrane forms a single, continuous compartment (Thylakoid membrane) which resembles stacks of flattened disks and the disks are called grana (singular, granum).

By the process of photosynthesis, chlorophylls and other molecules in the thylakoid membrane harness the energy in sunlight to drive the synthesis of ATP. The ATP is then used inside the stroma to build carbohydrates from carbon dioxide and water.

**Chloroplast structure**:

- **Two outer membranes** enclose a fluid called the **stroma**, which contains enzymes and the chloroplast's **own DNA**.
- Inside the stroma is a third, highly folded membrane system, the **thylakoids**, stacked like coins. Each stack is a **granum** (plural **grana**).

How photosynthesis uses them: chlorophyll in the **thylakoid membranes** captures sunlight and uses its energy to make **ATP**; that ATP is then used in the **stroma** to build **carbohydrates from carbon dioxide and water**.

slides.title: ENERGY RELATED ORGANELLE: MITOCHONDRIA & CHLOROPLAST
notes: Mitochondria and chloroplasts have similarities with bacteria:
Double membrane envelope
Free ribosome and circular DNA
Independent growth and reproduction
They may have evolved from ancient bacteria that were engulfed but not digested.
Mitochondria and chloroplasts developed because as a prokaryote it gained protection by living inside the eukaryote and in turn produced energy for the eukaryote (symbiotic relationship).

slides.explanation:
Mitochondria and chloroplasts look like **bacteria living inside cells**:

- **double membrane** envelope
- their **own ribosomes and circular DNA**
- they **grow and reproduce independently**

The idea that they evolved from ancient bacteria that were engulfed but not digested is called the **endosymbiotic theory**. It was a win-win (**symbiosis**): the bacterium gained protection inside the host, and the host gained energy.

slides.title: LOCOMOTOR APPENDAGES: CILIA & FLAGELLA
notes: Cilia – Cilia (singular, cilium) are short, hair-like structures that project from the surface of some cells. Mainly found in eukaryotic cells.
The coordinated waving of many cilia propels cells through fluid, and stirs fluid around stationary cells.
Flagella –Flagella are long hair-like structure and present in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells.

In prokaryotes flagellum projects from the cell wall and enables a cell to move. In eukaryotes, flagellum structure is different from the prokaryotic cells and whip back and forth to propel cells such as sperm through fluid. They have a different internal structure and type of motion than flagella of bacteria.

slides.explanation:
**Cilia and flagella** are hair-like structures for movement:

- **Cilia**: **short** and numerous, mainly in eukaryotic cells. Their coordinated beating moves cells through fluid or moves fluid past cells that stay still (for example, clearing mucus in the airways).
- **Flagella**: **long**, found in both **prokaryotes and eukaryotes**. A eukaryotic flagellum **whips back and forth** (like a sperm cell's tail); a bacterial flagellum projects from the cell wall and **rotates**, with a completely different internal structure.

Lipid bilayers are the basic structural and functional framework of all cell membranes, gives membrane it's fluidity

The nucleus is separated from the cytoplasm by a double membrane (two phospholipid bilayers); known as the nuclear envelope.
Many ribosomes are attached to the endoplasmic reticulum. Areas of rough ER are active sites of protein production.

Many ribosomes are also found floating freely in the cytoplasm wherever proteins are being assembled. Cells that are actively producing protein (e.g., liver cells) have great numbers of free and attached ribosomes.
The cytoskeleton is a network of fibers extending throughout the cytoplasm.
Part of the cytomembrane system is an extension of the nuclear envelope called endoplasmic reticulum, or ER.
The Golgi is a series of flattened membrane compartments, whose purpose is to process and package proteins produced in-the rough endoplasmic reticulum.
Digestion & recycling centers

Inside the stroma, a third, highly folded membrane forms a single, continuous compartment (Thylakoid membrane) which resembles stacks of flattened disks and the disks are called grana (singular, granum).

slides.explanation: Lecture 10 is about the **central dogma of life**: how the information stored in DNA is turned into proteins, in two steps called **transcription** and **translation**. It connects the nucleic acids and proteins from Lectures 6–7 with the nucleus and ribosomes from Lectures 8–9.

Genes specify proteins via transcription and translation
The central dogma of biology describes the flow of information from gene sequence to protein product

slides.explanation:
The big idea in five steps:

- DNA stores information as a **sequence of nucleotides** (bases).
- That sequence decides which **proteins** a cell makes, and proteins produce an organism's **traits**.
- **Gene expression** is the process by which DNA directs protein synthesis. It has **two stages: transcription and translation**.
- The **central dogma** describes this one-way flow of information: **DNA → RNA → protein**.

Exam tip: be able to write the flow and name both stages.

slides.title: An Analogy
notes: When you get to the library, you search through the shelves until you find a book that has a good set of instructions for making a table.
The library doesn't have a photocopier, but you came well-prepared and you whip out your pen and notebook and copy down (or 'transcribe') the instructions.
Satisfied, you take your notes and head back home.
At home, you have all the wood and tools to make the table.
You follow the instructions and make the table, effectively 'translating' the written words into a table which you can use in your room.

The library analogy makes the central dogma easy to remember. You find a book in the library with instructions for making a table. You cannot take the book home, so you **copy (transcribe)** the instructions into your notebook. At home, you use wood and tools to follow the instructions and build the table, **translating** words into an object.

Mapping the analogy onto the cell:

- **Library** = nucleus
- **Books** = DNA, packaged as chromosomes
- **One chapter** = one **gene** (instructions for one protein)

The key point: DNA stays in the nucleus, so an mRNA copy carries the message out.

slides.explanation:
**Basic principles**:

- **RNA is the bridge** between genes and the proteins they code for.
- **Transcription**: making **RNA** from the information in **DNA**. It produces **messenger RNA (mRNA)**.
- **Translation**: making a **polypeptide (protein)** from the information in **mRNA**. It happens at the **ribosomes**.

Memory tip: *transcribe* means to copy in the same language (DNA and RNA are both nucleotides); *translate* means to change language (nucleotides into amino acids).

The complete pathway in a eukaryotic cell:

1. **Transcription**: DNA → pre-mRNA, in the **nucleus**.
2. **RNA processing**: pre-mRNA → mature **mRNA**, in the nucleus.
3. mRNA leaves the nucleus into the **cytoplasm**.
4. **Translation**: a **ribosome** reads the mRNA and builds a **polypeptide**.

slides.title: Transcription
notes: DNA sequence information is converted to mRNA in a process called transcription
Steps:
1. The double-stranded DNA molecule is partially unzipped
An enzyme called RNA polymerase copies the gene's nucleotides one by one into an mRNA molecule.
Like DNA, mRNA is made of a particular sequence of nucleotides
Unlike DNA, mRNA has only a single strand, and the base Thymine in DNA is replaced by Uracil in RNA
Very importantly, mRNA is small and can easily exit the nucleus and go to the cytoplasm, where proteins are made.

slides.explanation:
**Transcription** converts a DNA sequence into an mRNA sequence:

1. The double-stranded DNA is **partly unzipped** at the gene.
2. The enzyme **RNA polymerase** copies the gene's bases one by one into an **mRNA** molecule, using complementary base pairing.

How mRNA compares with DNA:

- Like DNA, it is a sequence of nucleotides.
- Unlike DNA, it is **single-stranded**, and **uracil (U) replaces thymine (T)**.
- It is **small**, so it can leave the nucleus for the cytoplasm.

slides.title: Translation
notes: The sequence encoded in the mRNA molecule is decoded and converted to an amino acid sequence in a process called translation.
Steps:
After a mature mRNA leaves the nucleus of a cell, it heads for a ribosome in the cell’s cytoplasm where the code it contains can be translated to produce a protein
As the strand of mRNA slides through the ribosome, the code is read three nucleotides at a time (called a codon).
Each codon specifies one amino acid in the polypeptide chain of a protein which are linked together to form a protein.

slides.explanation:
**Translation** decodes the mRNA into a chain of amino acids:

1. Mature mRNA leaves the nucleus and attaches to a **ribosome** in the cytoplasm.
2. The ribosome reads the mRNA **three bases at a time**. Each group of three is a **codon**.
3. **Each codon specifies one amino acid**. The amino acids are joined in order by peptide bonds to form a polypeptide, which folds into a protein.

Exam tip: a codon is three nucleotides on the **mRNA**, coding for one amino acid.

slides.explanation:
**Cellular respiration** is the process by which cells **break down glucose** and **release the chemical energy stored in it**. In eukaryotic cells it happens mainly in the **mitochondria**.

Because glucose reacts with oxygen and is broken down, respiration is like a slow, controlled **burning**, which is why it is called **oxidation**.

Don't confuse **respiration** (a chemical process inside cells) with **breathing** (moving air in and out of the lungs).

slides.explanation:
Breathing and cellular respiration are linked but different:

- **Breathing** brings **oxygen** into the body and removes **carbon dioxide**.
- **Cellular respiration** uses that oxygen with **glucose** (from food) to produce **carbon dioxide, water and energy**.

So breathing supplies the ingredients and removes a waste product; respiration is the reaction itself.

slides.explanation: Respiration is often compared with **burning**: both combine fuel with oxygen and release energy, carbon dioxide and water. The difference is that burning releases the energy all at once as heat and light, while respiration releases it **step by step**, controlled by enzymes, so the cell can capture much of it as **ATP**.

The overall equation for cellular respiration:

Is it anabolic or catabolic? It breaks a large molecule into small ones and releases energy, so it is **catabolic**.

slides.explanation:
**Catabolism vs anabolism** in detail:

- **Catabolism**: **breaks down** complex molecules into simple ones; it is **oxidative and degradative** and **releases energy** (captured as ATP from ADP, and NADH from NAD⁺). Starting materials are varied and complex; the products are few and simple.
- **Anabolism**: **builds** complex, useful molecules from simple ones and **uses energy** (from ATP).

Respiration is catabolic; photosynthesis and protein synthesis are anabolic.

slides.explanation:
**ATP (adenosine triphosphate)** is the cell's main **energy currency**. Cells cannot use energy from glucose directly; instead they **store it in ATP**, which can **quickly release** it wherever it is needed.

Think of glucose as a large bank note and ATP as small change: easy to spend on the cell's many small jobs.

Breaking of each bond releases 7 kilo-calories of energy.

slides.explanation:
The structure of ATP is written **A–Ⓟ~Ⓟ~Ⓟ**:

- **A** = adenosine
- each **Ⓟ** = one **phosphate group**
- each **~** = a **high-energy phosphate bond**

Breaking one of these high-energy bonds releases about **7 kilocalories** of energy (per mole). The energy of ATP is stored in its phosphate bonds, especially the last one.

slides.explanation:
How ATP releases energy:

**ATP → ADP + Ⓟ + energy** (A–Ⓟ~Ⓟ~Ⓟ → A–Ⓟ~Ⓟ + Ⓟ)

Removing the last phosphate turns ATP into **ADP (adenosine diphosphate)** and releases energy. This powers most energy-using jobs in the cell: **nerve signals, muscle movement, protein synthesis** and **cell division**.

ADP is then **recharged** into ATP using energy from food in cellular respiration. This is the **ATP–ADP cycle**, like recharging a battery.

**Lactic acid fermentation** is the other type. During **heavy exercise**, muscles may not get oxygen fast enough for aerobic respiration, so muscle cells switch to anaerobic respiration:

slides.explanation:
**Enzymes** are biological **catalysts**, usually proteins, that **speed up reactions** in living cells which would otherwise be far too slow.

- The molecule an enzyme acts on is its **substrate**.
- The enzyme binds the substrate to form a short-lived **enzyme–substrate complex**.
- After the reaction, the complex splits into the **products** and the **unchanged enzyme**.

The diagram shows how an enzyme works. The substrate fits into a special pocket on the enzyme called the **active site**, forming the **enzyme–substrate (E–S) complex**. The reaction happens, the **products** are released, and the enzyme is free to work again.

This is often described as a **lock and key**: only the right substrate fits the active site.

slides.title: The Chemical nature of enzymes
notes: Enzymes are specific: each enzyme usually catalyses only one type of reaction.
Enzymes combine with their substrates to form temporary enzyme-substrate complex.
Enzymes are not altered or used up by the reactions they catalyze, so can be used again and again.
Enzymes are sensitive to temperature and pH.
Many enzymes need cofactors in order to function.
Enzyme function may be slowed down or stopped by inhibitors.

slides.explanation:
Properties of enzymes:

- **Specific**: each enzyme usually catalyses only **one type of reaction** (its active site fits one substrate).
- They form a **temporary enzyme–substrate complex**.
- They are **not used up or changed**, so they can be used again and again.
- They are **sensitive to temperature and pH**: too hot or the wrong pH changes their shape and stops them working.
- Many need **cofactors** (helper molecules or ions).
- They can be slowed or stopped by **inhibitors**.

Most digestive enzymes are hydrolases.
Lyase: these catalyze the break down of molecules by reactions that do not involved hydrolysis.
Isomerase: These catalyze the transformation of one isomer into another
Ligase: These catalyze the formation of bonds between compounds, often using the free energy made available from ATP hydrolysis.

slides.explanation:
Enzymes are classified into **six groups** by the reaction they catalyse:

1. **Oxidoreductases**: oxidation and reduction reactions
2. **Transferases**: transfer a chemical group from one compound to another
3. **Hydrolases**: hydrolysis (splitting with water); most **digestive enzymes** are hydrolases
4. **Lyases**: break molecules apart **without** water
5. **Isomerases**: convert one **isomer** into another
6. **Ligases**: **join** compounds, often using energy from ATP

The name ending *-ase* marks an enzyme.

slides.explanation:
All living things need a **continuous supply of energy**, and almost all of it comes from the **Sun**.

Green organisms capture the Sun's energy and store it in the chemical bonds of **glucose**. This process is **photosynthesis**. Every other organism depends on that stored energy, directly or through food chains (the energy pyramid from Lectures 1–2).

slides.explanation:
Two ways of getting food:

- **Autotrophs** (*self-feeders*) make their own food from simple substances around them, using **light** (photosynthesis) or **chemical energy** (chemosynthesis). Examples: green plants, algae, some bacteria.
- **Heterotrophs** (*other-feeders*) **cannot** make their own food and must eat other organisms, plants or animals. Examples: animals, fungi, most bacteria.

**Glucose** (C₆H₁₂O₆) is the **basic unit of energy** for living things and the single unit (monosaccharide) of the carbohydrate family. It contains carbon plus hydrogen and oxygen in the same 2:1 ratio as water, which is why it can be written C₆(H₂O)₆.

**Chlorophyll** is found in the **chloroplasts**. It captures light energy that drives the photosynthesis reaction (the slide describes it as working like a catalyst that speeds up the process; strictly, it is a light-absorbing pigment rather than an enzyme).

Other pigments help by absorbing colours chlorophyll misses and passing the energy on:

- **Carotenes**: orange
- **Xanthophylls**: yellow

These become visible in autumn leaves when chlorophyll breaks down.

slides.explanation:
**Photosynthesis vs respiration**, the take-home comparison:

- **Photosynthesis** makes food: **CO₂ + H₂O → carbohydrate + O₂**, using sunlight and chlorophyll. It **absorbs CO₂**, **releases O₂**, **stores energy**, and happens in **chloroplasts** of green cells in light.
- **Respiration** breaks food down: **glucose + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O + energy**. It **absorbs O₂**, **releases CO₂**, **releases energy**, and happens in the **mitochondria** of all living cells, day and night.

The two processes are roughly opposite and complement each other.

Why cells divide:

- **All cells come from pre-existing cells** (the third part of the cell theory).
- New cells are needed for **growth** and to **replace damaged or old cells**.

The way cells divide **differs** between **prokaryotes** (bacteria), which use binary fission, and **eukaryotes** (protists, fungi, plants and animals), which use mitosis and meiosis.

**Eukaryotic** cells store their genetic information in several **chromosomes** inside the nucleus. Most eukaryotes have **10 to 50** chromosomes in their body cells.

**Human body cells have 46 chromosomes, arranged as 23 pairs.** In each pair, one chromosome comes from the mother and one from the father. The slide calls them identical pairs; strictly they are **homologous** pairs: they carry the same genes but may carry different versions of them.

slides.explanation:
Cells cannot divide forever: after a certain number of divisions they die by **programmed cell death (apoptosis)**. At any moment some cells are dividing and some are dying. The balance changes with age:

- **Childhood**: division **>** death, so the body grows.
- **Adulthood**: division **=** death, so size stays steady.
- **Aging**: division **<** death, so tissues slowly decline.

slides.explanation:
Prokaryotes such as bacteria divide by **binary fission** (*binary* = two, *fission* = splitting):

1. The single **chromosome replicates** (makes a copy).
2. The cell grows, and the two chromosomes move apart.
3. A new **cell wall and membrane form between** them.
4. The cell **splits** into **two identical daughter cells**.

There is no mitosis, because there is no nucleus.

slides.explanation:
The **five phases of the cell cycle**:

- **G1**: first growth phase (the cell grows and works normally)
- **S**: **synthesis**, when the **DNA is replicated**
- **G2**: second growth phase (preparing to divide)
- **M**: **mitosis**, division of the nucleus
- **C**: **cytokinesis**, division of the cytoplasm

G1, S and G2 together are called **interphase**, which takes about **90%** of the cycle. Exam tip: DNA is copied in S phase, not in mitosis.

- **Diploid (2n)**: two copies of each chromosome, as in body cells.

Facts about **meiosis**:

- It is preceded by **interphase**, when the chromosomes are replicated (just as before mitosis).
- It has **two divisions**: **meiosis I** and **meiosis II**.
- It is called **reduction division** because it halves the chromosome number.
- It starts with one **diploid (2n)** cell and produces **four haploid (n)** daughter cells.

More facts about **meiosis**:

- Each daughter cell has **half** the chromosome number of the original cell.
- It produces the **gametes**: eggs and sperm.
- In **males** it happens in the **testes** (**spermatogenesis**, making sperm).
- In **females** it happens in the **ovaries** (**oogenesis**, making eggs).

slides.explanation:
Why do we need meiosis? It is the **basis of sexual reproduction**.

At **fertilisation**, two **haploid (n)** gametes, a sperm and an egg, fuse to form a **diploid (2n) zygote**. If gametes were diploid, the chromosome number would double every generation. Meiosis prevents this by halving it first.

- **Haploid sperm**: 1n = 3
- **Haploid egg**: 1n = 3
- They fuse → **diploid zygote**: 2n = 6

For humans the numbers are 23 + 23 = 46.

slides.explanation:
The logic of meiosis in one line: **meiosis halves the chromosome number; fertilisation restores it**.

Mother (2n) → egg (n) + father (2n) → sperm (n) → child (2n). Without the halving step, each generation would have twice the genetic content of the one before, far too much. With it, every generation has **the right number**.

slides.explanation:
Two **types of reproduction**:

- **Asexual**: **one parent**; a single cell or organism divides to make **identical** offspring. Examples: **binary fission, budding**.
- **Sexual**: **two cells (egg and sperm) join** to form a **zygote** that is **not identical** to either parent. Meiosis produces the gametes it needs.

The remaining slides describe the forms of asexual reproduction.

slides.title: Asexual reproduction
notes: Binary Fission:
Binary fission is the simplest form and involves the division of a single organism into two complete organisms, each identical to the other and to the parent.

Fission is common among unicellular organisms such as bacteria, many protists, some algae such as Spirogyra and Euglena, as well as a few higher organisms such as flatworms and certain species of polychaete worms.

slides.explanation:
**Binary fission** is the simplest form of asexual reproduction: one organism divides into **two complete organisms**, identical to each other and to the parent.

It is common in **unicellular** organisms: **bacteria**, many **protists**, some algae (such as *Spirogyra* and *Euglena*), and even a few multicellular animals such as **flatworms** and some polychaete worms.

slides.title: Asexual reproduction
notes: Regeneration:
A similar form of asexual reproduction is regeneration, in which an entire organism may be generated from a part of its parent.
The term regeneration normally refers to re-growth of missing, or damaged body parts in higher organisms, but whole body regeneration occurs in Hydra, starfish, and many plants.

slides.explanation:
**Regeneration** is a form of asexual reproduction in which a **whole new organism grows from a part** of the parent.

In most higher animals, regeneration only means **regrowing a missing or damaged part** (like a lizard's tail from Lectures 1–2). But in **Hydra, starfish** and many **plants**, a piece can regrow into an entire new organism.

slides.title: Asexual reproduction
notes: Asexual Spore:
Spores are another form of asexual reproduction and are common among bacteria, protists, and fungi.
Spores are DNA-containing capsules capable of sprouting into new organisms; unlike most seeds, spores are produced without sexual union of gametes, that is, reproductive cells.

slides.explanation:
**Asexual spores** are DNA-containing capsules that can **sprout into new organisms**. They are common in **bacteria, protists and fungi** (think of the spores of bread mould).

Unlike most seeds, spores are produced **without the union of gametes**, so no sexual process is involved.

slides.title: Asexual reproduction
notes: Budding:
Budding is another method of asexual reproduction in which a group of self-supportive cells sprouts from and then detaches from the parent organism.
Unlike eggs or spores, buds are multicellular and usually contain more than one cell layer.
Hydra and sea squirts reproduce by budding.

slides.explanation:
**Budding**: a group of cells **grows out from the parent** as a bud, then **detaches** to live independently.

Unlike eggs or spores, a bud is **multicellular**, usually with more than one layer of cells. **Hydra** and **sea squirts** reproduce this way (yeast, a single-celled fungus, also buds).

slides.title: Asexual reproduction
notes: Vegetative Reproduction:
Vegetative reproduction is common among plants and consists of certain parts that grow out from a main parent plant and eventually root and sprout to form new, independent plants.
Examples are the runners of strawberries, the tubers of potatoes, and the bulbs of onions.
Parthenogenesis:
Parthenogenesis is an important means of asexual reproduction in which new individuals are formed from unfertilized eggs.
It occurs in some insects, amphibians, reptiles, and birds and in some species of plants.

slides.explanation:
Two more types of asexual reproduction:

- **Vegetative reproduction** (common in plants): parts of the parent plant grow out, root and become new independent plants. Examples: strawberry **runners**, potato **tubers**, onion **bulbs**.
- **Parthenogenesis**: new individuals develop from **unfertilised eggs**. It happens in some insects (like aphids and bees), amphibians, reptiles, birds and some plants.

Exam tip: be able to name each type of asexual reproduction with one example.

slides.explanation: Lecture 15 is about **homeostasis**: how the body keeps its internal conditions steady even when the outside world changes. It ties together many organ systems, with **body temperature control** as the main worked example.

slides.title: Homeostasis
notes: The basic living unit of the body is the cell. The entire body contains about 100 trillions of cells.
About 60-80% of the adult human body is fluid. The cells of ours are bathed in this fluid termed as tissue fluid- a watery solution of ions and the other substances.
Tissue fluid forms the internal environment in which human body cells live.
The maintenance of nearly constant internal environment in side the body is called Homeostasis.

Homeostasis

slides.explanation:
The body is made of about **100 trillion cells**, and **60–80%** of an adult body is **fluid**. Cells are bathed in **tissue fluid**, a watery solution of ions and other substances. This fluid is the **internal environment** the cells live in.

**Homeostasis** is keeping this internal environment **nearly constant** (temperature, water, salts, glucose, pH and so on).

Exam tip: learn the one-line definition of homeostasis word for word.

slides.title: Control of Homeostasis
notes: Homeostasis is controlled by feedback mechanism.
The feedback mechanism consist of three parts:
1. A sense organ
2. A control centre (usually the brain)
3. A responding organ

slides.explanation:
Homeostasis is controlled by **feedback mechanisms** with **three parts**:

1. a **sense organ** (receptor) detects a change,
2. a **control centre**, usually the **brain**, compares it with the normal value and decides what to do,
3. a **responding organ** (effector) acts to correct the change.

The response is fed back: once conditions return to normal, messages tell the effector to **slow down or stop**. This is **negative feedback**, the standard mechanism of homeostasis.

slides.explanation:
Many organs share the work of homeostasis:

- **lungs** and respiratory tract (gases)
- **heart** and circulatory system (transport)
- **liver, pancreas** and gut (nutrients, glucose)
- **kidneys** (water, salts, wastes)
- **musculoskeletal system** (movement, heat from shivering)
- **skin** (temperature)
- **nervous system** and **endocrine glands** (control and coordination)

The next slides describe several of these in turn.

slides.explanation:
The **heart and circulatory system** are the body's delivery network:

- the heart **pumps blood** to all tissues and **maintains blood pressure**,
- blood brings **nutrients and oxygen** to cells,
- blood carries **carbon dioxide** away,
- blood takes **metabolic wastes** to the **kidneys** for filtering.

Without circulation, no other organ could keep the tissue fluid steady.

slides.title: Kidneys
notes: Kidneys keep blood and tissue fluid clean by filtering the substance not needed by the cells.

These substances include different end products of cellular metabolism, such as urea and uric acid; they also include excesses of ions and water from the food that might have accumulated in the extracellular fluid.
This controls the amounts of dissolved substances in the blood and tissue fluid, a process called osmoregulation. This is important for two reasons.
If the tissue fluid becomes too concentrated, cells will lose water by osmosis and become dehydrated.
And if it becomes too dilute, cells will take the excess water by osmosis.

For instance, when we drink a lot of liquid, the water content of our blood rises. This is detected by special sense organs and our kidneys respond by increasing the amount of water in the urine. As a result, a greater amount of more dilute urine is excreted until the water level in the tissue fluid returns to normal.

The **kidneys** keep blood and tissue fluid clean. They filter out what cells do not need: **wastes** such as **urea and uric acid**, and **excess ions and water**.

Controlling the amount of water and dissolved substances is **osmoregulation**. It matters because:

- if tissue fluid is **too concentrated**, cells **lose water** by osmosis and dehydrate;
- if it is **too dilute**, cells **take in too much water**.

Example: after drinking a lot, receptors detect the extra water, and the kidneys make **more, dilute urine** until water levels return to normal. (Link to osmosis in Lectures 4–5.)
