slides.title: Nervous system
notes: The nervous system consists of three major parts: the sensory input portion, the central nervous system, and the motor output portion.
Sensory receptors detect the body or the state of the structure of the surroundings. For instance, the eyes are sensory organs that give one a visual image of the surrounding area.

The central nervous system is composed of the brain and the spinal cord. The brain can store information, generate thoughts, create ambition, and determine reactions that the body performs in response to the sensations.
Appropriate signals are then transmitted through the motor output portion of the nervous system to carry out one’s desire.

The **nervous system** has **three major parts**:

1. **Sensory input**: receptors (such as the eyes) detect the state of the body and its surroundings.
2. **Central nervous system** (the **brain and spinal cord**): stores information, generates thoughts, and decides how to respond.
3. **Motor output**: carries signals to muscles and glands to carry out the response.

These map neatly onto the feedback loop: sense organ, control centre, responding organ.

slides.title: Endocrine glands
notes: Located in the body are eight major endocrine glands that secrete chemical substances called hormones.
Hormones are transported into the extracellular fluid to all parts of the body to help regulate cellular function.

For instance, thyroid hormone increases the rates of most chemical reactions in all cells, thus helping to set the tempo of bodily activity. Insulin controls glucose metabolism. Adrenocortical hormones controls Na+, K+ and protein metabolism. Parathyroid hormone controls bone calcium and phosphate.
Thus, the hormones are a system of regulation that complements the nervous system.
The nervous system regulates mainly muscular and secretory activities of the body, whereas the hormonal system regulates mainly metabolic functions.

The body has **eight major endocrine glands** that secrete **hormones**: chemical messengers carried through body fluids to regulate cells. Examples:

- **thyroid hormone**: raises the rate of chemical reactions, setting the body's pace,
- **insulin**: controls **glucose** metabolism,
- **adrenocortical hormones**: control **Na⁺, K⁺** and protein metabolism,
- **parathyroid hormone**: controls bone **calcium and phosphate**.

The two systems complement each other: the **nervous system** mainly controls **muscles and secretion** (fast), while **hormones** mainly control **metabolism** (slower, longer lasting).

slides.explanation:
Temperature regulation as a **feedback loop**:

1. **Stimulus**: body temperature rises above normal.
2. **Receptors**: temperature sensors in the skin and in the hypothalamus detect it.
3. **Control centre**: the thermoregulatory centre in the hypothalamus.
4. **Effectors**: **sweat glands** secrete more; **blood vessels** in the skin widen.
5. **Response**: more heat lost by evaporation and radiation, so **normal temperature is restored**.

This cycle is the standard example of negative feedback.

slides.explanation:
How the **TRC** works:

1. It **receives information** about body temperature.
2. It **sends signals** to adjust heat loss or heat production and keep core temperature steady.
3. Information comes from **thermoreceptors** (temperature sensors); the body has two kinds, in the **skin** and in the **core**.
4. These thermoreceptors send their signals to the TRC.

In other words: sensors → TRC → corrective response.

slides.explanation:
The skin has **three main layers**:

- **Dermis**: the middle layer; holds the skin's **appendages** (hair follicles, glands, nerves, blood vessels).

slides.title: Epidermis
notes: Epidermis, is the outermost layer of the skin. It forms the waterproof, protective wrap over the body's surface. The epidermis contains no blood vessels, and is nourished by diffusion from the dermis. Epidermis is divided into several layers where cells are formed through mitosis at the innermost layers.
Dermis:

The dermis is the layer of skin beneath the epidermis that consists of connective tissue and cushions the body from stress and strain. The dermis is tightly connected to the epidermis by a basement membrane. It also harbors many nerve endings that provide the sense of touch and heat. It contains the hair follicles, sweat glands, sebaceous glands, apocrine glands, lymphatic vessels and blood vessels.

- **Dermis**: **connective tissue** beneath the epidermis that **cushions** the body. It holds **nerve endings** (touch, heat), **hair follicles, sweat glands, sebaceous (oil) glands**, lymphatic vessels and **blood vessels**.

Exam tip: blood vessels are in the dermis, not the epidermis.

slides.title: Hypodermis
notes: The hypodermis is not part of the skin, and lies below the dermis. Its purpose is to attach the skin to underlying bone and muscle as well as supplying it with blood vessels and nerves. It consists of loose connective tissue and elastin. The main cell types are fibroblasts, macrophages and adipocytes (the hypodermis contains 50% of body fat). Fat serves as padding and insulation for the body.

slides.explanation:
When the body is **too cold**:

- **sweating stops**,
- blood vessels in the skin **narrow (vasoconstriction)**, so less blood flows near the surface and less heat is lost,
- muscles start rapid, jerky contractions: **shivering**, which **produces extra heat**.

Compare with the previous slide: the responses to heat and cold are opposites.

slides.title: Fever and hyperthermia
notes: 1. Fever occurs when the core temperature of the body is raised above normal steady state levels. The body reacts as if it is too cold, while the temperature rises up to the new higher set point. Fever attacks imply shivering combined with vasoconstriction, headache, body pains, and general discomfort.

slides.explanation:
**Fever** is a rise in core temperature above the normal level. The body's **set point** is raised, so the body **reacts as if it were too cold** while its temperature climbs to the new, higher set point.

That is why a fever attack brings **shivering** and **vasoconstriction** (feeling cold), along with headache, body aches and discomfort.

4. Following an attack of fever, vasodilatation and sweat evaporation reduces the core temperature.

slides.explanation:
How fever happens:

- Microbes release **exogenous pyrogens** (outside fever-causing substances).
- These make the body's defence cells release **endogenous pyrogens**, which act on the hypothalamus and **raise the temperature set point** through **prostaglandins**.
- **Antipyretic drugs** (fever reducers such as aspirin) block the enzyme **cyclo-oxygenase**, which stops prostaglandins being made.
- When the fever breaks, **vasodilation and sweating** bring the temperature back down.

A **pyrogen** is any substance, such as a heat-stable bacterial toxin, that causes a rise in body temperature.

slides.explanation: The body can also lose **too much heat**. Anyone not properly protected from the cold can develop **hypothermia** (body temperature colder than normal) or **frostbite** (tissue damage from freezing, usually in fingers, toes, ears and nose).

slides.title: Hypothermia
notes: Hypothermia occurs when the body temperature falls below 95 degrees F. The normal body temperature is 98.6 degrees F. In the early stages, this may cause memory loss, confusion and shivering. Eventually, a low body temperature may cause cardiac arrest and death.
The best way to prevent hypothermia is to protect the body from the cold.

slides.explanation:
**Hypothermia** is when body temperature falls **below 95 °F (35 °C)**; normal is about **98.6 °F (37 °C)**.

Early signs: **shivering, confusion and memory loss**. As it gets worse, low temperature can cause **cardiac arrest and death**. The best prevention is simply to **protect the body from the cold**.

Exam tip: fever raises the set point; hypothermia is heat loss beating heat production.

slides.explanation:
**Digestion** is the process that converts food into substances the body can **absorb and assimilate** (use to build itself). It combines **mechanical** breakdown (chewing, churning) and **chemical** breakdown (enzymes).

The four macromolecules in food are broken into their building blocks (from Lectures 6–7):

- nucleic acids → **nucleotides**
- proteins → **amino acids**
- fats → **fatty acids and glycerol**
- carbohydrates → **simple sugars**

Minerals, vitamins and water are also taken from food along the way.

slides.title: Food Sources
notes: Biologists categorize animals into three groups based on their food source.
Herbivores obtain all food from plants. Examples:cows, horses, and nearly all rodents.
Carnivores obtain all food from meat.
Examples: cats, eagles, wolves, and frogs.
Omnivores obtain food from both plants and meat. Examples: humans and bears.

An animal’s digestive system is specifically suited to processing food obtained from its food source. For example, herbivores’ digestive systems are equipped to break down plant material, and carnivores’ are not.

slides.explanation:
Animals are grouped by **food source**:

- **Herbivores** eat only **plants** (cows, horses, most rodents).
- **Carnivores** eat only **meat** (cats, eagles, wolves, frogs).
- **Omnivores** eat **both** (humans, bears).

Each animal's digestive system is suited to its diet. Plant material is hard to digest, so herbivores have long, specialised guts to break it down, while carnivores do not.

slides.title: Digestive system(Tract)
notes: The digestive tract is the area where digestion takes place.
The digestive tract varies widely in complexity from species to species.
The most primitive form found in nematodes is simply a tubular gut with no specialized features.
The slightly more advanced digestive tract found in earthworms includes specialized areas for ingestion, storage, fragmentation, digestion, and absorption.
The most advanced digestive tracts, found among the vertebrates,exhibit specialization on a much greater scale.

slides.title: Human Digestive system
notes: The human alimentary canal:
The alimentary canal begins at the mouth and the pharynx.
From here, food travels down a muscular tube called the esophagus and into the stomach.
The stomach connects to the small intestine, which in turn connects to the large intestine.
Some form of mechanical and chemical digestion breaks down food at every step along this tube and Nutrients are absorbed across the walls of both intestines.
All products remaining after food travels through the large intestine are waste, which exit the body through the anus.

slides.explanation:
Digestion starts in the **mouth (oral cavity)**:

- **Teeth** break food into smaller pieces, giving enzymes more **surface area** to work on (mechanical digestion).
- The **tongue** moves food and shapes it into a **bolus**, a soft ball that is easy to swallow.
- **Salivary glands** secrete **saliva**, which contains water, salt and the enzyme **salivary amylase**. Amylase begins breaking **starch into smaller sugars** (chemical digestion). Saliva also contains **buffers** that neutralise acidic food and **antibacterial substances**, and it lubricates food for swallowing.

Sphincter muscles at each end prevent backflow.
The wall of the digestive tube is composed of 4 basic layers:

slides.explanation:
The **stomach** is a sac-like organ with a folded inner lining that lets it **stretch** when full.

**Gastric glands** in the lining secrete **gastric juice**, an **acidic** mixture of enzymes and mucus. Two cell types matter:

- **Parietal cells** secrete **hydrochloric acid (HCl)**.
- **Chief cells** secrete **pepsinogen**, the inactive form of the enzyme **pepsin**.

HCl makes the stomach very acidic, about **pH 2**, which starts protein digestion. Exam tip: parietal = acid, chief = pepsinogen.

slides.title: Structure and functions of components of Human Digestive System
notes: The Stomach (Contd.)
Low pH levels are necessary for pepsinogen to be converted into the active digestive enzyme pepsin, which further breaks down food proteins.
If chief cells were to secrete pepsin directly into the stomach, the pepsin would digest the cells themselves.
Additionally, mucus lines the stomach walls and prevents it from being digested.
A mixture of gastric acid and partially digested food called chyme passes out of the stomach.

More on the stomach:

- **Low pH** converts inactive **pepsinogen** into active **pepsin**, which breaks proteins down.
- Why release pepsinogen and not pepsin? If chief cells made active pepsin, it would **digest the cells themselves**.

slides.title: Structure and functions of components of Human Digestive System
notes: The Small Intestine (Contd.)
The small intestine is split into three sections:
the duodenum, jejunum, and the ileum.
Chemical digestion takes place in the duodenum and the jejunum.
The ileum, the final section of the small intestine, is where most absorption of the nutrients takes place.
Small projections called villi cover the ileum walls.
Cells lining the villi are covered in folds of plasma membrane that form even smaller projections called microvilli.
Villi and microvilli increase the ileum’s surface area, providing more surface across which nutrients can be absorbed.
Nutrients pass through capillaries in the lining of the villi and into the bloodstream, where they circulate first to the liver, then throughout the rest of the body.
Villi and microvilli projections also contain digestive enzymes to further digest food.

slides.explanation:
The **small intestine** has **three sections**: **duodenum, jejunum and ileum**.

- **Chemical digestion** happens mainly in the **duodenum and jejunum**.
- The **ileum**, the last section, is where much of the **absorption** of nutrients happens.

The walls are covered in finger-like **villi**, whose cells carry even smaller projections called **microvilli**. Together they hugely **increase the surface area** for absorption. Absorbed nutrients enter **capillaries** in the villi and travel **first to the liver**, then to the rest of the body.

slides.explanation:
Most **chemical digestion and absorption** happen in the **small intestine**. **Bile salts** break fats into small droplets, while **pancreatic fluid** containing **bicarbonate neutralises** the acid chyme from the stomach.

Enzymes and what they digest:

- **Starch**: pancreatic amylase, maltase, sucrase, lactase
- **Protein**: trypsin, chymotrypsin, aminopeptidase, carboxypeptidase
- **Nucleic acids**: nucleases
- **Fats**: bile salts and lipase

Note: the slide says the duodenum controls the release of food into the small intestine; in most textbooks this is the job of the **pyloric sphincter** at the end of the stomach.

slides.title: Structure and functions of components of Human Digestive System
notes: The Large Intestine
Food from the small intestine empties into the large intestine, or colon.
No digestion and only a small percentage of absorption take place in the large intestine.
The large intestine primarily functions to concentrate waste material into a form called feces.
Movements of the large intestine compact feces and move it into the rectum, where it is exited from the body through the anus.
Feces is expelled from the body through the voluntary movements of muscles surrounding the rectum.

The **large intestine (colon)** receives what is left from the small intestine.

- Its movements compact the faeces and push them into the **rectum**; they leave through the **anus** under **voluntary** muscle control.

- **Gallbladder**: **stores bile** and squirts it into the small intestine when fat arrives.

slides.explanation:
The **liver** is the **largest internal organ** and is called the body's **chemical factory**:

- It **processes the nutrients** absorbed from the small intestine (remember, blood from the gut goes to the liver first).
- It makes **bile**, which is important for **digesting fat**.
- It turns absorbed raw materials into the many **chemicals the body needs**.

The **gallbladder** is a pear-shaped organ that **stores about 50 mL of bile** until it is needed. It is linked to the liver and duodenum by the biliary tract, and it **concentrates bile** between meals.

2. It **removes wastes**, such as bilirubin, which leave the body in faeces.

slides.explanation:
The **pancreas** is a leaf-shaped organ near the stomach and duodenum. It secretes **pancreatic juice** into the duodenum:

- **Amylase**: starch → glucose (via smaller sugars)
- **Protease** (e.g. trypsin): proteins → polypeptides
- **Lipase**: fats → fatty acids + glycerol
- **Bicarbonate**: neutralises the **acidic chyme** from the stomach.

It is also an endocrine gland: it secretes **insulin** directly into the blood, the chief hormone for handling sugar (see Lecture 19 on diabetes).

slides.explanation:
The human **circulatory system** is the combined work of the **heart, blood and blood vessels** (arteries, veins and capillaries). Its job is to **transport oxygen and nutrients** to every organ and tissue and to **carry away waste products**.

Exam tip: this one-sentence definition names all three parts; learn it.

slides.title: Circulatory System- Vital Functions
notes: Increases the flow of blood to meet increased energy demands during exercise and regulates body temperature.

When foreign substances or organisms invade the body, the circulatory system swiftly conveys disease-fighting elements of the immune system, such as white blood cells and antibodies, to regions under attack.
In the case of injury or bleeding, the circulatory system sends clotting cells and proteins to the affected site, which quickly stop bleeding and promote healing.

slides.explanation:
Beyond transport, circulation has other vital jobs:

- **Exercise and temperature**: it increases blood flow when energy demand rises and helps **regulate body temperature**.
- **Defence**: it rushes **white blood cells and antibodies** to where microbes have invaded.
- **Healing**: after an injury, it sends **platelets and clotting proteins** to stop bleeding and start repair.

slides.explanation:
The circulatory system has **four basic structures**:

1. a **fluid tissue**: **blood** (and lymph)
2. a **network of tubing**: **arteries and veins**
3. **specialised tubing**: **capillaries**, thin enough for molecules to **diffuse** in and out
4. a **pump**: the **heart**, which keeps blood moving

slides.explanation:
How the heart's parts work together:

- The two **atria collect** blood returning to the heart.
- The two **ventricles pump** blood out of the heart.
- **Valves** stop blood flowing backwards.
- The **septum** is the wall separating the left and right sides.
- The **right side** pumps **deoxygenated** blood to the **lungs**.
- The **left side** pumps **oxygenated** blood to the **rest of the body**.

Memory tip: **right = lungs, left = body**. The left ventricle has the thickest wall because it pumps furthest.

slides.title: Anatomy- Heart
notes: The walls of these chambers are made of a special muscle called MYOCARDIUM, which contracts continuously and rhythmically to pump blood.
The pumping action of the heart occurs in two stages for each heartbeat:
(1) DIASTOLE, when the heart is at rest; and
(2) SYSTOLE, when the heart contracts to pump deoxygenated blood toward the lungs and oxygenated blood to the body.
During each heartbeat, typically about 60 to 90 ml of blood are pumped out of the heart. If the heart stops pumping, death usually occurs within four to five minutes.

slides.explanation:
The heart's walls are made of special muscle, the **myocardium**, which contracts continuously and rhythmically.

Each heartbeat has two stages:

- **Diastole**: the heart **relaxes** and fills with blood.
- **Systole**: the heart **contracts**, pumping deoxygenated blood to the lungs and oxygenated blood to the body.

Each beat pumps about **60–90 mL** of blood. If the heart stops, death follows within about **four to five minutes**, because the brain is starved of oxygen.

slides.explanation:
**Normal blood pressure** in adults:

- **Systolic** (pressure while the heart contracts): **90–120 mmHg**
- **Diastolic** (pressure while it relaxes): **60–80 mmHg**

Blood pressure is written as systolic over diastolic, for example **120/80 mmHg**.

slides.title: Blood Vessels
notes: Arteries
Arteries are tubes that carry oxygenated blood away from the heart.
Arteries carry blood under the highest pressure (around 16 kPa).
The structure of an artery must be able to handle both high pressure and the changes in pressure that result from the rhythmic pumping of the heart.
Therefore, arteries are thick-walled, wrapped with elastic muscle tissue. Small arteries are called arterioles.

slides.explanation:
**Arteries** carry blood **away from the heart**, usually oxygenated.

- They carry blood under the **highest pressure** (around 16 kPa, about 120 mmHg).
- They must cope with that pressure and with its rise and fall on every heartbeat, so they have **thick walls** with **elastic muscle tissue**.
- The smallest arteries are **arterioles**.

slides.title: Blood Vessels
notes: Veins
Veins are tubes that return deoxygenated blood to the heart.
Veins provide a return system for blood under lower pressure that the blood in the arteries.
Therefore, the walls of veins do not need to be as thick or elastic as those of arteries.
The pressure of the blood coming out of the venous end of some capillaries often is not high enough to push the blood all the way back to the heart
For this reason, some veins in the legs and arms have one-way valves to ensure that the blood travels only toward the heart. Small veins are called venules.

slides.explanation:
**Veins** carry blood **back to the heart**, usually deoxygenated.

- Blood in veins is under **lower pressure**, so their walls are **thinner and less elastic** than arteries.
- The pressure left after the capillaries is often too low to push blood all the way back up to the heart, so veins in the arms and legs have **one-way valves** that stop blood flowing backwards. Nearby muscles squeeze the veins and help.
- The smallest veins are **venules**.

slides.explanation:
**Capillaries** connect arterioles to venules. They are a fine network of tiny, **thin-walled** tubes where **exchange** happens:

- **nutrients and oxygen** leave the blood and reach the cells,
- **cell wastes** (such as CO₂) diffuse back into the blood.

Only capillaries are thin enough for this exchange, so every living cell is close to one.

slides.title: The Pathway of Blood Circulation
notes: Blood returning to the heart from the arms, head, abdomen, and legs has little oxygen left in it.
As a result, the pathway that the blood follows should put more oxygen into the blood and then direct the re-oxygenated blood back out to the body tissues.
Systemic circulation is the movement of blood between the heart and the rest of the body.
Pulmonary circulation is the movement of blood between the heart and lungs.
Each of these circuits requires its own pump.
The pulmonary circuit uses the right half of the heart;
the systemic circuit uses the left half.

slides.explanation:
Blood returning from the body has **little oxygen left**, so it must be **re-oxygenated** before going out again. That is why there are **two circuits**:

- **Systemic circulation**: between the **heart and the rest of the body**.
- **Pulmonary circulation**: between the **heart and the lungs**.

Each needs its own pump: the **right half** of the heart drives the **pulmonary** circuit and the **left half** drives the **systemic** circuit. Humans therefore have a **double circulation**.

slides.title: Function of Blood
notes: Blood performs many important functions within the body including:
Supply of oxygen to tissues (bound to hemoglobin which is carried in red cells)
Supply of nutrients such as glucose, amino acids and fatty acids (dissolved in the blood or bound to plasma proteins)
Removal of waste such as carbon dioxide, urea and lactic acid
Immunological functions, including circulation of white cells, and detection of foreign material by antibodies
It maintains acid base balance, body temperature.
Messenger functions, including the transport of hormones and the signaling of tissue damage.

**Atherosclerosis** (a form of arteriosclerosis): fatty deposits called **plaques** build up on the **inner walls of arteries**. The arteries **narrow**, which **raises blood pressure** and increases the risk of **heart attack, stroke and kidney damage**.

This links back to the trans fats and cholesterol in Lectures 4–7.

Interruption of oxygen supply to the heart
Causes death of the heart muscle
Leading cause of death in both men and women
Stroke
Strokes usually result from rupture or blockage of arteries in the head
Brain cells are starved of oxygen and nutrients
Loss of function may occur
Can cause paralysis, loss of ability to speak or death.

slides.explanation:
Two major results of blocked arteries:

- **Heart attack** (acute **myocardial infarction**): the **oxygen supply to part of the heart muscle is cut off**, and that muscle **dies**. It is a leading cause of death in men and women.
- **Stroke**: an artery in the **brain** is **blocked or bursts**, so brain cells are **starved of oxygen and nutrients**. It can cause loss of function, **paralysis**, loss of speech or death.

slides.explanation:
How arteries get blocked, step by step:

1. **Cholesterol** sticks to the artery wall, so the artery **narrows** and blood slows.
2. Cholesterol makes the wall **rough**, so blood **clots** as it flows past. A clot can block the artery completely; this blockage is a **thrombosis**, and blood flow stops.
3. Bits of cholesterol can **break off** into the bloodstream and block narrower vessels elsewhere.

Globulins (designated alpha, beta, and gamma) transport various substances in the blood.
Many beta globulins bind to lipid (fat) molecules, such as cholesterol. When a protein attaches to one of these molecules, it creates a complex called a lipoprotein.
Two medically important lipoproteins are the low-density lipoproteins (LDLs) and high-density lipoproteins (HDLs).

slides.explanation:
**Red blood cells** are small, flat, **disc-shaped** cells with a **thinner centre** (biconcave). This shape makes them **flexible** enough to squeeze through tiny capillaries and gives a large surface for gas exchange.

They are red because of **haemoglobin**, an **iron**-containing protein that is red in colour. Mature human red cells also have no nucleus, leaving more room for haemoglobin.

slides.title: Red blood cell
notes: Red blood cells carry oxygen to body tissues and remove carbon dioxide (which bound with hemoglobin).
The process by which red blood cells are produced is called erythropoiesis.
Erythrocytes are continuously being produced in the bone marrow of large bones, at a rate of about 2 million per second. (In the embryo, the liver is the main site of red blood cell production).
In an adult, the total count of RBC is 4.5 to 5.5 million per mm3 of blood.

There are 150,000 to 300,000 platelets in each milliliter of blood.
Without blood platelets, you would bleed to death.
Platelets survive for 10 days before being removed by the liver and spleen.

- They live about **10 days** before being removed by the **liver and spleen**.

How platelets stop bleeding:

1. When a vessel is cut, platelets **stick to the edges** of the cut and to each other, forming a **plug**.

- **O– is the universal donor**: its red cells carry **no A, B or Rh antigen**, so it can be given to people of any blood type.

Exam tip: the donor is about the **antigens on the red cells** being given; the recipient is about the **antibodies in the plasma** receiving them.

slides.title: Introduction
notes: All animals must exchange gases between themselves and their environment on a continual basis.
Simple animals exchange gases throughout their entire body surfaces, whereas more complex animals have respiratory systems.
Complex organisms rely on breathing to simultaneously move oxygen gas from the air into the body and remove carbon dioxide from the body and return it to the air.
Respiration is the entire process of taking air in, exchanging oxygen for carbon dioxide and releasing air out.

slides.explanation:
All animals must **exchange gases** with their surroundings all the time.

- **Simple animals** (like flatworms) exchange gases across their **whole body surface**.
- **Complex animals** need a dedicated **respiratory system**.

Complex organisms rely on **breathing** to move oxygen into the body and carbon dioxide out at the same time. The slide defines **respiration** broadly here as the whole process of taking air in, swapping oxygen for carbon dioxide, and letting air out.

slides.explanation:
Most animals are **aerobic**: they need **oxygen**. **Carbon dioxide** matters too, because too much of it is harmful (it makes body fluids acidic).

The **respiratory and circulatory systems work together** to deliver oxygen to cells and remove carbon dioxide, in **two phases**:

- **Inhalation** (bringing oxygen in)
- **Exhalation** (sending carbon dioxide out)

slides.title: Gas Exchange and Breathing
notes: Inhalation
Inhalation brings air from outside the body into the lungs.
Oxygen in the air moves from the lungs through blood vessels to the heart, Heart pumps the oxygen-rich blood to all parts of the body.
Oxygen then moves from the bloodstream into cells, which completes the first phase of respiration.
In the cells, oxygen is used in a separate energy-producing process called cellular respiration, which produces carbon dioxide as a by-product.

slides.explanation:
**Phase 1: inhalation**

1. Air is breathed into the **lungs**.
2. Oxygen passes from the lungs into blood vessels and travels to the **heart**.
3. The heart pumps this **oxygen-rich blood** to the whole body.
4. Oxygen moves from the blood into the **cells**.

Inside the cells, oxygen is used in **cellular respiration**, which releases energy and produces **carbon dioxide** as a by-product.

slides.title: Gas Exchange and Breathing
notes: Exhalation
The second phase of respiration begins with the movement of carbon dioxide from the cells to the bloodstream.
The bloodstream carries carbon dioxide to the heart, which pumps the carbon dioxide-laden blood to the lungs.
In the lungs, breathing out, or exhalation, removes carbon dioxide from the body, thus completing the respiration cycle.

slides.explanation:
**Phase 2: exhalation**

1. **Carbon dioxide** moves from the cells into the **bloodstream**.
2. The blood carries it to the **heart**, which pumps it to the **lungs**.
3. **Breathing out (exhalation)** removes carbon dioxide from the body.

This completes the respiration cycle, which then repeats with every breath.

slides.title: Cellular Respiration vs. Breathing
notes: Cellular Respiration is the process by which living cells break down foods and release the stored chemical potential energy.
Breathing is the means by which respiratory gases are exchanged between the entire organism and its environment.

Breathing is simply a mechanical process. Breathing causes air containing a high concentration of oxygen to enter the lungs and cause air containing a high concentration of carbon dioxide to leave the lungs.

slides.explanation:
**Cellular respiration vs breathing**, which are often confused:

- **Cellular respiration** is a **chemical** process inside cells: food is broken down to **release stored energy**.
- **Breathing** is a **mechanical** process for the whole organism: it moves air rich in **oxygen into the lungs** and air rich in **carbon dioxide out**.

Breathing supplies the oxygen that cellular respiration uses, and removes the carbon dioxide it produces.

slides.title: Upper Respiratory Tract
notes: 1. Nasal Passages
The uppermost portion of the human respiratory system, the nose is a hollow air passage that functions in breathing and in the sense of smell.
The nasal cavity moistens and warms incoming air, while small hairs and mucus filter out harmful particles and microorganisms.
2. Pharynx
Air leaves the nasal passages and flows to the pharynx, a short, funnel-shaped tube about 13 cm (5 in) long that transports air to the larynx.

**Upper respiratory tract**:

1. **Nasal passages**: the nose is a hollow air passage used for **breathing and smell**. The nasal cavity **warms and moistens** incoming air, while small **hairs and mucus filter out** dust and microorganisms.
2. **Pharynx**: a short, **funnel-shaped tube** (about **13 cm**) that carries air from the nasal passages to the larynx. (It is also part of the pathway for food.)

slides.title: Lower Respiratory Tract
notes: 3. Larynx
Air moves from the pharynx to the larynx, a structure about 5 cm (2 in) long located approximately in the middle of the neck.
4.Trachea, Bronchi, and Bronchioles

Air passes from the larynx into the trachea, a tube about 12 to 15 cm (about 5 to 6 in) long located just below the larynx. The trachea branches into two tubes, the left and right bronchi, which deliver air to the left and right lungs, respectively. Within the lungs, the bronchi branch into smaller tubes called bronchioles.

**Lower respiratory tract**:

3. **Larynx**: about **5 cm** long, in the middle of the neck; it holds the vocal cords (the **voice box**).
4. **Trachea, bronchi and bronchioles**: air passes from the larynx into the **trachea** (about **12–15 cm** long). The trachea splits into the **left and right bronchi**, one to each lung. Inside the lungs, the bronchi branch into smaller tubes called **bronchioles**.

slides.title: Lower Respiratory Tract
notes: 5. Lungs
The two branches of the trachea, called bronchi, subdivide within the lobes into smaller and smaller air vessels. They terminate in alveoli, tiny air sacs surrounded by capillaries.

When the alveoli inflate with inhaled air, oxygen diffuses into the blood in the capillaries to be pumped by the heart to the tissues of the body, and carbon dioxide diffuses out of the blood into the lungs, where it is exhaled.

slides.explanation:
5. **Lungs**: inside the lung lobes, the airways keep branching into smaller and smaller tubes, ending in **alveoli**: tiny **air sacs** surrounded by **capillaries**.

When the alveoli fill with inhaled air:

- **oxygen diffuses** from the alveoli **into the blood**, to be pumped to the tissues;
- **carbon dioxide diffuses** from the blood **into the alveoli**, to be breathed out.

The alveoli are where gas exchange actually happens.

slides.explanation: **CO₂ out**: the heart pumps **deoxygenated** blood (poor in O₂, rich in CO₂) into the capillaries around the alveoli. Fresh air contains only about **0.034% CO₂**, far less than the blood. Because CO₂ concentration is **lower inside the alveolus**, CO₂ **diffuses from the blood into the air space** and is exhaled.

slides.title: Gas Exchange in Lungs
notes: Fresh inhaled air in the airspace contains about 21% oxygen. This is a very high concentration compared to what is in the blood.
Therefore, oxygen molecules diffuse from the airspace into the blood stream through the thin lining of the alveolus.
The now bright red, oxygen-rich blood moves through the capillary into the pulmonary vein and back to the heart.
At the same time that oxygen diffusion is occurring, carbon dioxide is diffusing from the blood into the air space of the alveolus.

**O₂ in**: fresh inhaled air contains about **21% oxygen**, a much higher concentration than in the blood, so **oxygen diffuses from the air space into the blood** through the **thin lining** of the alveolus.

The blood, now **bright red and oxygen-rich**, flows through the capillary into the **pulmonary vein** and back to the heart. CO₂ is diffusing out at the same time, so both exchanges happen together.

If you **hold your breath**, the air in the alveoli stops being refreshed, the concentration differences disappear, and **diffusion slows and stops**.

- **Water vapour**: 1% inhaled → **6%** exhaled

Exhaled air has **less oxygen** and **more CO₂ and water**. These numbers are common MCQ targets.

slides.explanation:
How **red blood cells carry oxygen**:

1. Red cells **pick up oxygen** as blood passes through the lungs.
2. Oxygen joins **haemoglobin** to form **oxyhaemoglobin**, which is **bright red**.
3. Around the body, oxyhaemoglobin **breaks down and releases oxygen** to the cells.
4. Without its oxygen, the blood is **dull red**, and it is pumped back to the lungs for more.

At the same time, tissues release CO₂ into the blood to be carried back to the lungs.

slides.explanation:
The **kidneys** are the body's main **excretory organs** and the main part of the **urinary system**, which has four parts:

1. **Kidneys**: **form urine**
2. **Ureters**: **carry urine** from the kidneys to the bladder
3. **Urinary bladder**: **stores urine** (a reservoir)
4. **Urethra**: carries urine from the bladder **out of the body**

Exam tip: don't mix up ureter (kidney to bladder) and urethra (bladder to outside).

slides.explanation:
**Functions of the kidneys**:

- **excretion** of excess substances and **metabolic wastes** (such as urea)
- **osmoregulation**
- regulation of **water and electrolyte balance**, **acid–base balance (pH)** and **blood pressure**

**Osmoregulation** is the process by which cells and organisms keep their **fluid and electrolyte balance** steady. (Link to homeostasis, Lecture 15, where the kidneys adjust urine volume after you drink a lot.)

slides.title: How kidneys clean blood
notes: Kidneys clean blood by filtering it. They filter all our blood 300 times a day. The filtering is done by over a million tubes packed into each kidney. These tubes are called nephrones.
Some people’s kidneys are not very good at filtering blood. Kidney machines help by filtering blood for them.
slides.rawText:
How kidneys clean blood

Kidneys clean blood by filtering it. They filter all our blood 300 times a day. The filtering is done by over a million tubes packed into each kidney. These tubes are called nephrones. 
Some people’s kidneys are not very good at filtering blood. Kidney machines help by filtering blood for them.
slides.ocrText:
How kidneys clean blood
• Kidneys clean blood by filtering it. They filter all our

million tubes packed into each kidney. These tubes are

• Some people's kidneys are not very good at filtering

slides.explanation:
The kidneys clean blood by **filtering** it, through the million or so tiny tubes in each kidney called **nephrons**. According to the lecture, they filter all of our blood about **300 times a day**.

When kidneys fail and cannot filter blood well, a **kidney (dialysis) machine** can filter the blood for them.

slides.title: What is Diabetes Mellitus?
notes: Normal Glucose Metabolism

When the amount of glucose in the blood increases, e.g., after a meal, it triggers the release of the hormone insulin from the pancreas. Insulin stimulates muscle and fat cells to remove glucose from the blood and stimulates the liver to metabolize glucose, causing the blood sugar level to decrease to normal levels.
Diabetes Mellitus
Diabetes mellitus is a metabolic disorder characterized by abnormally high levels of sugar (glucose) in the blood.
Condition of high levels of glucose in the blood is called Hyperglycemia.
Hereditary and Environmental causes.

slides.explanation:
**Normal glucose metabolism**: after a meal, blood glucose rises. This triggers the **pancreas** to release **insulin**. Insulin makes **muscle and fat cells take up glucose** and makes the **liver** use and store it, so blood sugar falls back to normal.

**Diabetes mellitus** is a **metabolic disorder** with **abnormally high blood glucose**. High blood glucose is called **hyperglycaemia**. It has both **hereditary** (genetic) and **environmental** causes.

slides.title: Causes of Hyperglycemia
notes: Insulin is a hormone secreted from the islet cells of the Pancreas.
Insulin enables cells to absorb glucose in order to turn it into energy, thereby keeping the normal blood glucose level in the blood.
In diabetes, blood sugar levels remain high, may be because insulin
is not being produced at all is not made at sufficient levels, or is not as effective as it should be.
This causes glucose to accumulate in the blood, often leading to various complications.

slides.explanation:
**Insulin** is a hormone made by the **islet cells of the pancreas** (the beta cells). It lets cells **absorb glucose** and turn it into energy, which keeps blood glucose normal.

In diabetes, blood sugar stays high because insulin is:

- **not produced at all**,
- **not produced in sufficient amounts**, or
- **not working as well as it should**.

Glucose then builds up in the blood and, over time, causes complications (damage to eyes, kidneys, nerves and blood vessels).

Type I or insulin dependent diabetes often called juvenile onset diabetes, Type II or non-insulin dependent diabetes often called adult onset diabetes & Gestational diabetes.
The most common forms of diabetes are type 1 diabetes
(5%), which is an autoimmune disorder. and Type 2 diabetes (95%), which is associated with obesity.
Gestational diabetes is a form of diabetes that occurs in pregnancy.

slides.explanation:
There are **three main types of diabetes**:

- **Type 1** (insulin-dependent, **juvenile-onset**): about **5%** of cases; an **autoimmune** disorder.
- **Type 2** (non-insulin-dependent, **adult-onset**): about **95%** of cases; associated with **obesity**.
- **Gestational diabetes**: occurs during **pregnancy**.

Note: the slide says the most common forms are type 1, but its own percentages show **type 2 is by far the most common**.

slides.title: Type 1 diabetes
notes: most commonly occurs in children is a result of the body's immune system attacking and destroying the beta islet cells.
The trigger for this autoimmune attack is not clear, but the result is the end of insulin production.
Type 2 diabetes
Type 2 diabetes commonly occurs in adults who are obese.
There are many underlying factors that contribute to the high blood glucose levels in these individuals.
An important factor is the body's resistance to insulin in the body, essentially ignoring its insulin secretions.
A second factor is the falling production of insulin by the beta cells of the pancreas.
Therefore, an individual with type 2 diabetes may have a combination of deficient secretion and deficient action of insulin.

slides.explanation:
**Type 1 diabetes** usually starts in **children**. The body's own **immune system attacks and destroys the beta cells** of the pancreatic islets. The trigger is unclear, but the result is that **insulin production stops**.

**Type 2 diabetes** usually occurs in **obese adults**. Two factors combine:

1. **Insulin resistance**: the body's cells respond poorly to insulin, effectively ignoring it.
2. **Falling insulin production** by the beta cells.

So type 2 is a mix of **deficient secretion and deficient action** of insulin. Exam tip: type 1 = no insulin; type 2 = insulin that doesn't work well.

slides.explanation:
Gestational diabetes also puts the **baby** at risk of:

- **Macrosomia**: a baby much **larger than normal** (extra glucose crosses to the baby and is stored as fat).
- **Birth injury**: because of the baby's large size and a difficult birth.
- **Hypoglycaemia**: **low blood sugar** in the baby right after delivery (the baby has been making extra insulin).
- **Respiratory distress**: difficulty breathing.

slides.explanation:
**Signs and symptoms of diabetes**:

- **dry mouth** and **extreme thirst**
- **frequent urination** (and bedwetting in children)
- **tiredness** all the time
- **sudden weight loss** and **constant hunger**
- **stomach pain**
- **wounds that won't heal**

Why? Excess glucose is lost in urine, taking water with it (thirst, urination), and cells can't use the glucose (hunger, tiredness, weight loss).

slides.explanation:
Diabetes is diagnosed by measuring blood glucose, either **fasting** (fasting plasma glucose test) or in an **oral glucose tolerance test** (OGTT, measured after a sugary drink). There are three categories, according to the lecture's table:

- **Normal**: fasting **< 115**, after a meal **< 140** mg/dL
- **Impaired glucose tolerance**: fasting < 140, after a meal **140–199** mg/dL
- **Diabetic**: fasting **> 140**, after a meal **> 200** mg/dL

Note: current international guidelines use lower fasting cut-offs (for example, diabetes at 126 mg/dL or above). For this course, use the lecture's table.

slides.rawText: Lipid profile

slides.explanation: The second part of the lecture: the **lipid profile**, the blood test for fats. It connects diabetes to heart disease, since people with diabetes are at higher risk of blocked arteries.

slides.title: What is a lipid profile?
notes: The lipid profile is a group of tests that are often ordered together to determine risk of coronary heart disease. The tests that make up a lipid profile are tests that have been shown to be good indicators of whether someone is likely to have a heart attack or stroke caused by blockage of blood vessels
(hardening of the arteries).

slides.explanation: A **lipid profile** is a group of blood tests ordered together to judge the **risk of coronary heart disease**. The tests have been shown to be good indicators of whether someone is likely to have a **heart attack or stroke** caused by blocked, **hardened arteries** (atherosclerosis, from Lecture 17).

slides.title: Your Lipid Profile
notes: When doctors order a lab test called a lipid profile (sometimes called a lipid panel), they are looking for information about the amounts of four types of fats in the blood. You will be asked to give a small sample of blood from your arm. The results can help your doctor evaluate your risk for heart disease.

slides.explanation: A lipid profile (also called a **lipid panel**) measures **four types of fat** in the blood. It needs only a small blood sample from the arm, and the results help a doctor estimate the patient's **risk of heart disease**.

slides.title: What tests are included in a lipid profile?
notes: The lipid profile includes total cholesterol, HDL-cholesterol (often called good cholesterol), LDL-cholesterol (often called bad cholesterol), and triglycerides.
Sometimes the report will include additional calculated values such as the Cholesterol/HDL ratio or a risk score based on lipid profile results, age, sex, and other risk factors.

The **lipid profile includes**:

1. **Total cholesterol**
2. **HDL cholesterol** ("good" cholesterol)
3. **LDL cholesterol** ("bad" cholesterol)
4. **Triglycerides**

Reports may also include calculated values such as the **cholesterol/HDL ratio** or a risk score that combines the results with age, sex and other risk factors.

slides.title: Slide 16
notes: Cholesterol helps the body form hormones, vitamin D and other important substances, but too much of it in the blood can clog and damage the blood vessels. Because it is a fat-like substance that doesn't mix with blood, cholesterol has to combine with proteins to form lipoproteins. Lipoproteins can travel in the blood to all the organs and tissues of the body.
Low-density lipoproteins (LDLs, or "bad" cholesterol) build up in the blood and increase your risk of heart disease.

**Cholesterol** is not all bad: the body uses it to make **hormones, vitamin D** and other important substances. But **too much** in the blood can **clog and damage** blood vessels.

Cholesterol is fat-like and doesn't mix with blood, so it travels combined with proteins as **lipoproteins**.

**LDL (low-density lipoprotein)** is **"bad" cholesterol**: it builds up in the blood and vessel walls and **raises heart disease risk**.

Triglycerides store energy for your body to use when it is needed. If there is too much, it can block blood vessels and cause other health problems such as abdominal pain and pancreatitis.

slides.explanation:
If you know **total cholesterol (TC)**, **triglycerides (TG)** and **HDL**, you can **estimate LDL** (the Friedewald formula):

**LDL = TC − HDL − TG/5** (all in mg/dL)

Example: TC 200, HDL 50, TG 150 → LDL = 200 − 50 − 30 = **120 mg/dL** ("good" range). Try making up a set of values and working it out.

Type 2 diabetes
Type 2 diabetes commonly occurs in adults who are obese.

An important factor is the body's resistance to insulin in the body, essentially ignoring its insulin secretions.
A second factor is the falling production of insulin by the beta cells of the pancreas.

Two key definitions:

- **Nutrition** is **all the processes** by which organisms **obtain and use** nutrients.

The lecture then covers the classes of nutrients, vitamins, calories, healthy weight and BMI, malnutrition, and reading food labels.

The percentages on the slide show roughly how much of the body each makes up: about **60% water** and about **20% fat**. Exam tip: the six classes are a very common list question.

slides.title: Energy Nutrients: Carbohydrates, Lipids and Proteins
notes: Used by body as source of energy.
All these three nutrients are Carbon containing compounds.
Proteins are not preferred energy source. They are building blocks to make our body.
Body does not get energy from vitamins, minerals, water.

slides.explanation:
**Energy nutrients** are the three the body can use as **fuel**: **carbohydrates, lipids and proteins**. All three are **carbon-containing** (organic) compounds.

- **Proteins are not the preferred energy source**; the body mainly uses them as **building blocks**.
- The body gets **no energy** from **vitamins, minerals or water**, even though it needs them.

slides.title: Carbohydrates
notes: Fresh fruits, whole grains, and vegetables—especially legumes such as peas and beans—provide abundant complex carbohydrates .
The body breaks the starch in these foods into glucose, your primary source of energy. These foods also provide essential vitamins and fiber.
Eating foods high in soluble fiber helps lower one's cholesterol level and may reduce the risk of heart disease.
A diet high in insoluble fiber helps prevent constipation.

Foods rich in processed carbohydrates such as white flour, refined sugar, and corn syrup are sometimes said to be "empty calories” This is a way of saying that these foods provide little in the way of vitamins or fiber.

**Carbohydrates**:

- Fruits, **whole grains** and vegetables (especially **legumes** such as peas and beans) provide **complex carbohydrates**. The body breaks their starch down into **glucose**, its **main energy source**. They also supply vitamins and fibre.
- **Soluble fibre** helps **lower cholesterol** and may reduce heart disease risk.
- **Insoluble fibre** helps **prevent constipation**.
- **Processed** carbohydrates (white flour, refined sugar, corn syrup) are called **"empty calories"**: plenty of energy but few vitamins or fibre.

slides.title: Lipids
notes: Body uses lipids to build cell membranes, as energy stores, and as a reservoir for fat-soluble vitamins.
Linoleic acid and alpha-linolenic acid are essential fatty acids, meaning the human body needs them but cannot make them.
Mainly 2 types: saturated and unsaturated fatty acids.
Dairy products and meats are rich in saturated fats and cholesterol. Overindulging in these foods increases one's risk for heart disease, stroke, and some cancers.
Trans fatty acids, or trans fats, are manufactured from vegetable oils.
Worse for the heart than saturated fats.

slides.explanation:
**Lipids**:

- The body uses them to build **cell membranes**, as **energy stores**, and as a store for **fat-soluble vitamins**.
- **Linoleic acid** and **alpha-linolenic acid** are the **essential fatty acids**: needed but not made by the body, so they must be eaten.
- Fatty acids are **saturated** or **unsaturated**. **Dairy and meat** are rich in **saturated fat and cholesterol**; too much raises the risk of heart disease, stroke and some cancers.
- **Trans fats**, made from vegetable oils, are **even worse for the heart than saturated fat** (see Lectures 4–5).

slides.title: Proteins
notes: Amino acids are building blocks of proteins.
Your cells can make some amino acids but you must get essential amino acids from food.
Most proteins in meat are "complete," meaning their amino acid ratios match a human's nutritional needs.
By contrast, most plant proteins are "incomplete," meaning they lack one or more amino acids essential for the human diet.

slides.explanation:
**Proteins** are built from **amino acids**. Your cells can make some amino acids, but the **essential amino acids must come from food**.

- Most **meat proteins are "complete"**: their amino acid mix matches human needs.
- Most **plant proteins are "incomplete"**: each lacks one or more essential amino acids. Eating a mix of plant proteins (for example rice with lentils) covers the gaps.

Many functions in body though required in small amount.

Humans need **13 essential vitamins**; the major groups are **A, B, C, D, E and K**. Vitamins are classified by whether they dissolve in **fat or water** (next slide).

Taken with fat containing foods.
They can remain stored in body fats.
Not necessary to consume everyday.
•2. Water soluble Vitamins: B and C.
Cannot be stored.
Need to take frequently/Everyday.
slides.explanation:
Two groups of vitamins:

- **Fat-soluble: A, D, E and K**. Absorbed with fatty foods, **stored in body fat**, so they **do not have to be eaten every day** (and too much can build up).
- **Water-soluble: B and C**. **Cannot be stored** (the excess leaves in urine), so they **must be taken frequently, ideally every day**.

Memory aid for fat-soluble: **"ADEK"**.

slides.explanation:
**Minerals** are **inorganic** substances carried around the body as **ions** dissolved in blood and other fluids. Each has its own roles, for example:

- **Calcium**: builds **bones and teeth** and helps **blood clot**.
- **Sodium**: maintains **fluid balance**.
- **Magnesium**: helps **release energy** from the energy nutrients.

(Iron, needed for haemoglobin, is another key example.)

slides.title: Water
notes: Water provides the medium in which all the body’s reactions take place.
It aids in the digestion and absorption of food.
It is a medium of transport, through arteries and veins, within an organism.
It even lubricates your joints and cushions organs such as the brain and spinal cord.
It helps in the excretion of harmful by-products of metabolic processes.
It aids in the regulation of heat loss.
Key players when bonds are broken (by hydrolysis) or formed (by dehydration synthesis) in these molecules.

slides.title: Food as Fuel: Calories Count
notes: Food energy is usually measured in kilocalories (kcal), also called Calories (Cal).
A large apple contains about 70 Cal worth of energy-producing compounds; and jogging 1.6 km (1 mile) burns about 100 Cal of stored energy.
The food energy in a slice of bread could bring a liter of water to a boil, and a pound of body fat has enough energy to bring 52 liters (13 gal) to a boil!
Each person has a minimum daily energy requirement that varies with age, sex, body size, activity level, and other factors.
In general, a normally active female college student needs around 1,800-2,000 Cal a day to fuel her total metabolic needs;
a male college student needs about 2,200-2,500 Cal.
Carbohydrate and protein each provide about 4 Cal/g, while fat provides more than twice as much, or 9 Cal/g.
A person would have to run for about 30 minutes, for example, to burn off the calories in a cheeseburger.

slides.explanation:
Food energy is measured in **kilocalories (kcal)**, also written **Calories (Cal)** with a capital C.

- A large apple has about **70 Cal**; jogging 1 mile (1.6 km) burns about **100 Cal**.
- Daily needs vary with age, sex, body size and activity: roughly **1,800–2,000 Cal** for an active female college student and **2,200–2,500 Cal** for a male.
- **Carbohydrate and protein give about 4 Cal/g; fat gives about 9 Cal/g**, more than twice as much.
- Burning off one cheeseburger takes about **30 minutes of running**.

slides.explanation:
The energy balance rule:

- **Food energy in > energy needed** → the extra is **stored as body fat** (weight gain).
- **Energy needed > food energy in** → the body **burns stored fat** (weight loss).

Weight stays steady only when intake matches use.

slides.explanation:
A **balanced diet** contains all the **proximate principles of food** (the main nutrient groups) in **adequate and proportionate amounts**, including essential amino acids and fatty acids, for normal growth, activity and reproduction.

- **Adequate** means the amount that supplies **exactly the calories** needed.
- **Proportionate** means the **right proportion** of each kind of food.

Exam tip: learn this definition with its two key words, adequate and proportionate.

- **enough fruit and vegetables**
- food that is **easily digested, absorbed and assimilated**

slides.explanation:
**Body Mass Index (BMI)**, also called the **Quetelet index**, is a value calculated from a person's **weight and height**:

**BMI = body mass (kg) ÷ height (m)²**

Its units are **kg/m²**. It is a quick screening tool for underweight and overweight.

slides.rawText: Body Mass Index(BMI) count
slides.ocrText:
Body Mass Index(BMI) count
Measurement
Units
Kilograms
and meters
(or
centimeters)
Formula and Calculation
Formula: weight (kg) / [height (m)]2
With the metric system, the formula for BMI is weight in kilograms divided
by height in meters squared. Since height is commonly measured in
centimeters, divide height in centimeters by 100 to obtain height in
meters.
Example: Weight = 68 kg, Height = 165 cm (1.65 m)
Calculation: 68 ÷ (1.65)2 = 24.98
slides.explanation:
Worked example of BMI:

- Weight = **68 kg**, height = **165 cm = 1.65 m** (divide cm by 100 to get metres)
- BMI = 68 ÷ (1.65)² = 68 ÷ 2.72 = **24.98 kg/m²**

That falls in the **normal** range (18.5–24.9), right at its upper edge. Exam tip: remember to **square the height in metres**.

slides.explanation:
A quick way to **estimate your daily kilocalorie needs**:

1. Multiply your weight **in pounds** by **10** if inactive, **15** if moderately active, or **20** if highly active.
2. Then **subtract** an amount that depends on your age (from the table on the slide), because energy needs fall as you get older.

slides.title: How To Calculate How Many Kilocalories You Need
notes: For example, if you are 25 years old, are highly active, and weigh 120 pounds, you will require 120 X 20 = 2,400 kilocalories daily to maintain weight. If you want to gain weight you will require more; to lose, you will require less. The amount is only a rough estimate.
Other factors, such as height, must be considered. A person 5 feet, 2 inches tall and active does not require as much energy as an active 6-footer whose body weight is the same.

slides.title: Malnutrition
notes: Malnutrition refers to insufficient, excessive, or imbalanced consumption of nutrients by an organism.
In developed countries, the diseases of malnutrition are most often associated with nutritional imbalances or excessive consumption.

Although there are more organisms in the world who are malnourished due to insufficient consumption, increasingly more organisms suffer from excessive over-nutrition; a problem caused by an over abundance of sustenance coupled with the instinctual desire (by animals in particular) to consume all that it can.
slides.rawText:
Malnutrition
Malnutrition refers to insufficient, excessive, or imbalanced consumption of nutrients by an organism.
 In developed countries, the diseases of malnutrition are most often associated with nutritional imbalances or excessive consumption.
Although there are more organisms in the world who are malnourished due to insufficient consumption, increasingly more organisms suffer from excessive over-nutrition; a problem caused by an over abundance of sustenance coupled with the instinctual desire (by animals in particular) to consume all that it can.

•Malnutrition refers to insufficient, excessive, or imbalanced

slides.explanation:
**Malnutrition** means **insufficient, excessive or imbalanced** intake of nutrients. It is not only hunger.

- In **developed countries**, malnutrition is mostly **imbalance or over-eating** (leading to obesity and related diseases).
- Worldwide, more individuals are malnourished from **too little** food, but a growing number suffer from **over-nutrition**: plenty of food combined with the instinct to eat as much as possible.
